status: Research draft; no catalogue edits or deployment
scope: 196 actual local development choices individually mapped; 497 source families inventoried separately. Live availability is not reverified in this research.
method: Exact identity, display metadata and variant description inspected. 148 available catalogue/reference images reviewed, including 94 buildings. No new GLB fidelity audit, architectural authorship authentication or whole-neighbourhood performance evaluation was performed.

classical.label: Classical and formal traditions
classical.explanation: Historic architectural languages that use balanced composition, formal detail or prominent rooflines.
classical.note: Keep the specific names visible: Neoclassical, Georgian, Italianate and Second Empire have different identifying features.

gothic_romantic.label: Gothic and Romantic revivals
gothic_romantic.explanation: Architecture that draws on medieval or castle-like forms to create a strong historical character.
gothic_romantic.note: Pointed arches, steep gables and turrets offer easy features for students to recognise.

decorative_modern.label: Art Nouveau and Art Deco
decorative_modern.explanation: Distinct decorative approaches associated with the turn of the twentieth century and the decades that followed.
decorative_modern.note: Show the differences: flowing craft, geometric ornament, or streamlined horizontal forms.

modern.label: Modernism and Brutalism
modern.explanation: Architecture that explores simple forms, function, materials and visible construction.
modern.note: Brutalism is a distinct branch; exposed concrete alone does not establish it.

contemporary.label: Contemporary architecture
contemporary.explanation: Recent architectural approaches with many different materials, shapes and design goals.
contemporary.note: Use short descriptors such as minimalist, timber or planted terraces when the model shows them.

regional.label: Regional and traditional architecture
regional.explanation: Buildings shaped by local traditions or familiar patterns of domestic life and craftsmanship.
regional.note: Keep local identities visible: machiya, Craftsman and Maritime houses should retain their own names.

industrial.label: Industrial and utilitarian design
industrial.explanation: Buildings and structures whose form responds strongly to work, large spans, storage or servicing.
industrial.note: Students can compare older iron-and-glass construction with contemporary working buildings.

review.label: Style to be confirmed
review.explanation: The reference or description needs checking before a specific style is taught.
review.note: This is an instructor review category, not a student architectural movement.

neoclassical.label: Neoclassical / Classical Revival
neoclassical.features: Symmetry, classical columns, ordered proportions and restrained geometric composition.
neoclassical.values: Clarity, order and continuity with antiquity; often used to project institutional permanence.
neoclassical.caution: Appearance does not establish a client’s politics; distinguish ornate Beaux-Arts work.

brutalism.label: Brutalism
brutalism.features: Expressive mass, deep openings and an overt presentation of materials, structure and construction.
brutalism.values: Material directness and a serious, legible architectural presence.
brutalism.caution: Concrete alone is insufficient; Brutalism also includes important brick and steel examples.

modernism.label: Modernism / International-style influence
modernism.features: Unornamented volumes, structural grids and extensive glazing.
modernism.caution: A recent building is not automatically a historical Modernist work; date and authorship require evidence.

contemporary.label: Contemporary architecture
contemporary.features: Current architectural vocabulary; specific examples differ in materials, roofs and composition.
contemporary.values: Discuss each design’s stated aims rather than assigning one shared ideology.
contemporary.caution: An umbrella for browsing, not a distinct historical movement.

minimalism.label: Minimalist contemporary
minimalism.features: Reduced material palette, plain volumes and carefully placed openings.
minimalism.values: Restraint, spatial clarity and emphasis on proportion.
minimalism.caution: Simplicity of appearance does not establish low cost or environmental performance.

timber_contemporary.label: Contemporary timber architecture
timber_contemporary.features: Visible timber frames, timber surfaces or a timber-led architectural composition.
timber_contemporary.values: Making construction legible and exploring material warmth.
timber_contemporary.caution: Timber is a material, not a style or an automatic carbon certification.

nordic.label: Nordic-inspired contemporary
nordic.features: In these catalogue examples: restrained palettes, timber and clear roof forms.
nordic.values: Use the examples to discuss domestic scale, light and material restraint.
nordic.caution: A local curatorial label, not a universal definition of Scandinavian architecture.

biophilic.label: Biophilic design
biophilic.features: Deliberate connections to planting, daylight, natural materials and natural forms.
biophilic.values: Strengthening people’s connection with nature in the built environment.
biophilic.caution: A planted roof or timber surface does not prove whole-building sustainability.

gothic.label: Gothic Revival / Gothic-inspired
gothic.features: Pointed openings, tracery, steep roofs and vertical accents.
gothic.values: Historical continuity and expressive craftsmanship; often spiritual or collegiate associations.
gothic.caution: A contemporary model using Gothic forms is not an original medieval building.

italianate.label: Italianate / Renaissance-inspired commercial
italianate.features: Bracketed cornices, arched openings and layered facade composition.
italianate.values: Civic or commercial dignity and an urban facade addressing the street.
italianate.caution: Close examples may combine Italianate and Renaissance Revival motifs.

georgian.label: Georgian / Georgian-influenced
georgian.features: Balanced facades, regularly arranged windows and a composed entrance.
georgian.values: Proportion, symmetry and an orderly domestic or civic presence.
georgian.caution: Contemporary adaptations and regional examples need not date from the Georgian period.

second_empire.label: Second Empire / mansard eclecticism
second_empire.features: Mansard roofs, dormers and an elaborate roof silhouette.
second_empire.caution: A mansard alone is not conclusive; later eclectic buildings also use it.

belle_epoque.label: Belle Époque eclectic / Beaux-Arts influence
belle_epoque.features: Richly articulated classical composition combined with iron, glass and other decorative vocabularies.
belle_epoque.caution: Belle Époque is a period; identify the actual Classical, Art Nouveau or other elements.

modernisme.label: Catalan Modernisme / Art Nouveau influence
modernisme.features: Decorative ironwork, coloured glass and expressive craft in these market references.
modernisme.values: Integration of architecture, craft and regional cultural expression.
modernisme.caution: Modernisme is distinct from twentieth-century International Modernism.

art_deco.label: Art Deco
art_deco.features: Geometric ornament, strong vertical accents and stepped composition.
art_deco.values: Modernity expressed through decoration, craft and visual energy.
art_deco.caution: Give Streamline Moderne its own subcategory rather than flattening the distinction.

moderne.label: Streamline Moderne
moderne.features: Rounded corners, smooth surfaces and strong horizontal bands.
moderne.caution: Related to Art Deco, with a distinct formal vocabulary.

baronial.label: Scottish Baronial Revival
baronial.features: Turrets, crow-stepped gables and a castle-like roofline.
baronial.values: Romantic historical identity and a picturesque silhouette.
baronial.caution: The railway-hotel family also includes other styles; label this exact variant.

craftsman.label: Arts and Crafts / Craftsman
craftsman.features: Expressed carpentry, substantial porch elements and legible construction.
craftsman.values: Craftsmanship, material care and a response to industrial standardisation.
craftsman.caution: A bungalow is a building type and can have several architectural styles.

edwardian.label: Edwardian / Foursquare, Classical influence
edwardian.features: In this example: square massing, a hipped roof, dormer and columned porch.
edwardian.values: An orderly domestic composition with restrained traditional detail.
edwardian.caution: Foursquare is a type; Edwardian is a period. The Classical influence is the stylistic observation.

vernacular.label: Regional vernacular / traditional urban
vernacular.features: Established local patterns of roofs, materials, entrances and adaptation.
vernacular.values: Everyday usefulness and continuity of local building knowledge.
vernacular.caution: Name the region and visible traits; avoid treating every older building as one historical style.

machiya.label: Traditional Japanese machiya
machiya.features: Timber construction, street-facing lattice and a relationship to interior gardens.
machiya.values: Continuity of living, work, craft and local urban culture.
machiya.caution: A converted café retains traditional identity; Japanese location does not mean contemporary style.

mediterranean.label: Mediterranean / Tuscan-inspired
mediterranean.features: For these models: arcades, stucco or stone, tiled roofs and sheltered outdoor rooms.
mediterranean.values: Shaded thresholds and relationships between indoor and outdoor life.
mediterranean.caution: A broad label; different regional traditions and modern adaptations should remain distinguishable.

ranch.label: Post-war Ranch / suburban vernacular
ranch.features: Low horizontal composition, broad roof and an informal street-facing domestic presence.
ranch.values: Ground-oriented living and a close relationship to the private plot.
ranch.caution: A house form does not determine the street network or require suburban sprawl.

industrial.label: Industrial / utilitarian architecture
industrial.features: Simple enclosures, working doors, repetitive bays and visible construction systems.
industrial.values: Efficient accommodation of work, storage and servicing.
industrial.caution: A metal shed or concrete warehouse is not automatically Brutalist or High-Tech architecture.

historic_industrial.label: Historic industrial / iron-and-glass
historic_industrial.features: Iron or steel frames, large spans, daylight glazing and brick enclosures.
historic_industrial.values: Structure and daylight organised around working or public interior space.
historic_industrial.caution: Distinguish original construction from a later adaptive-reuse intervention.

structural.label: Structural expression / High-Tech influence
structural.features: Exposed frames, bracing, cables or other structure as a main part of the composition.
structural.values: Making the way a building or bridge stands up visually legible.
structural.caution: Not every exposed structure belongs to the historical High-Tech movement.

rustic.label: Rustic / Parkitecture influence
rustic.features: Logs, stone and crafted shelter forms that relate to a landscape setting.
rustic.values: Blending built structures with their landscape.
rustic.caution: The NPS tradition is specific; use “influenced” for an unsourced contemporary analogue.

traditional_inspired.label: Traditional-inspired contemporary
traditional_inspired.features: Current buildings using familiar pitched roofs, porches and domestic proportions.
traditional_inspired.values: Familiarity and continuity of domestic form.
traditional_inspired.caution: A new traditional-looking home is not necessarily a surviving historic building.

classical_uncertain.label: Classical / eclectic — review needed
classical_uncertain.features: A formal facade, dome or classical motif appears in the reviewed reference.
classical_uncertain.values: Potential teaching themes: proportion and institutional presence.
classical_uncertain.caution: Conflicting variant text or imagery must be resolved before a precise student label is published.

contemporary_landscape.label: Contemporary public-space design
contemporary_landscape.features: Current arrangements of paving, seating, planting and public activity.
contemporary_landscape.values: Discuss the actual arrangement, use and experience of each space.
contemporary_landscape.caution: An umbrella, not one ideology or a named historical movement.

naturalistic.label: Naturalistic / picturesque-inspired landscape
naturalistic.features: Informal planting, varied views and paths composed around landscape scenery.
naturalistic.values: Restoration, discovery and attention to site character.
naturalistic.caution: Naturalistic appearance does not prove ecological restoration or Olmsted authorship.

formal_garden.label: Formal / gardenesque tradition
formal_garden.features: Ordered beds, designed paths, garden structures or deliberately displayed planting.
formal_garden.values: Cultivated display and a composed visitor experience.
formal_garden.caution: Victorian gardenesque, French formal gardens and contemporary geometric courts are not interchangeable.

japanese_garden.label: Japanese-inspired garden
japanese_garden.features: This reference combines a stream, stones, bridge and carefully framed planted views.
japanese_garden.values: Attention to sequence, detail and relationships among water, stones and planting.
japanese_garden.caution: Broad visual inspiration only; a specific Japanese garden school is not established.

ecological_landscape.label: Ecological / green-infrastructure landscape
ecological_landscape.features: Wetland planting, rain gardens or other designed relationships to water and habitat.
ecological_landscape.values: Connecting public landscape with environmental processes.
ecological_landscape.caution: Performance requires hydrology, soils and species evidence; the model is illustrative.

productive.label: Productive / community-growing landscape
productive.features: Fruit trees, allotments or demonstration planting organised for growing and learning.
productive.values: Stewardship, cultivation and opportunities for shared learning.
productive.caution: An orchard does not establish community ownership or food-system performance.

recreation.label: Sport / recreation design — no specific style
recreation.features: Courts, play or activity equipment and their supporting outdoor space.
recreation.values: Opportunities for recreation and social activity.
recreation.caution: Standard court dimensions do not establish an architectural style or planning ideology.

heritage_street.label: Traditional / historic streetscape
heritage_street.features: A fine-grained street frontage, traditional paving or a locally distinctive street pattern.
heritage_street.values: Continuity of urban character and street-based daily life.
heritage_street.caution: Historic precedents can inform several current planning approaches.

haussmann.label: Haussmannian boulevard tradition
haussmann.features: Broad tree-lined boulevards and a coordinated metropolitan street composition.
haussmann.values: Movement, infrastructure and a strong metropolitan image.
haussmann.caution: Teach the historical transformation as well as its attractive appearance.

canal.label: Canal-city streetscape tradition
canal.features: Waterways, narrow urban edges, planted quays and bridge crossings.
canal.values: Connections among water, movement and the urban edge.
canal.caution: A canal segment does not establish the whole city’s transport priorities.

contemporary_street.label: Contemporary street / public-realm design
contemporary_street.features: Current street arrangements with deliberate allocation of movement, planting and social space.
contemporary_street.values: Make the priorities visible by comparing the actual allocation of space.
contemporary_street.caution: Aesthetic planting alone does not demonstrate safe or inclusive operation.

engineering.label: Engineering / standard-section design
engineering.features: A prescribed road section, bridge structure or infrastructure component.
engineering.caution: A standard is not a planning ideology or proof of legal compliance.

surface.label: Path / surface component — style neutral
surface.features: A clear walking or cycling surface in a stated material.
surface.values: Connecting places and providing a legible route.
surface.caution: A path’s material cannot determine the planning ideology of a neighbourhood.

new_urbanism.label: New Urbanism — compatible component
new_urbanism.meaning: Compact, connected neighbourhoods combining different uses and housing choices.
new_urbanism.values: Walkable daily life and well-defined shared public space.
new_urbanism.limit: A compatible frontage or street is one component; a whole-plan assessment is needed.

tod.label: Transit-oriented development — compatible component
tod.meaning: Integrating land use with walking, cycling and useful public transport.
tod.values: Access to activities with less dependence on cars.
tod.limit: A station or tall building alone does not establish TOD, service quality or equitable outcomes.

compact.label: Compact infill / missing-middle approach
compact.meaning: Adding ground-oriented or modest-scale multi-unit homes and mixed-use buildings within an urban fabric.
compact.values: Housing variety and efficient use of serviced land.
compact.limit: Building form does not prove affordability, tenure or absence of displacement.

place.label: Public-life / placemaking principles
place.kind: Design and participatory approach / component affinity
place.meaning: Organising places around activities and the needs of the people who use them.
place.values: Comfort, sociability and meaningful local use.
place.limit: Benches and attractive paving do not establish a community-led placemaking process.

heritage.label: Heritage continuity / adaptive reuse
heritage.meaning: Retaining or adapting inherited buildings and urban patterns.
heritage.values: Continuity, cultural identity and reuse of existing fabric.
heritage.limit: A newly generated historic-looking model does not prove a real conservation project.

ecology.label: Ecological planning / green infrastructure
ecology.meaning: Treating water, habitat, planting and built development as related systems.
ecology.values: Resilience and care for environmental processes.
ecology.limit: Model appearance cannot establish stormwater capacity, biodiversity or carbon performance.

garden_city.label: Garden City principles — component affinity
garden_city.meaning: Combining settlement, landscape, local work and long-term community stewardship.
garden_city.values: Healthy living and shared community benefit.
garden_city.limit: Green space alone is not Garden City planning; land, governance, jobs and housing matter.

city_beautiful.label: City Beautiful / civic-composition affinity
city_beautiful.meaning: Coordinating civic buildings, axes and public spaces into a formal composition.
city_beautiful.values: Civic identity and a prominent public realm.
city_beautiful.limit: A single Classical building or symmetrical garden is insufficient evidence.

vancouverism.label: Vancouverism — tower-and-podium component
vancouverism.meaning: Slender towers combined with lower urban edges, public space and an emphasis on sustainable movement.
vancouverism.values: Density with attention to light, views and street life.
vancouverism.limit: The tower-and-podium model alone cannot establish public benefits or the neighbourhood framework.

haussmann.label: Haussmannian urbanism
haussmann.meaning: Metropolitan restructuring through boulevards, infrastructure and coordinated urban frontage.
haussmann.values: Connectivity and a deliberate city image.
haussmann.limit: A boulevard replica is an illustration of this tradition, not a reproduction of its social history.

complete.label: Complete Streets principles
complete.meaning: Allocating street space for safe access by people using different modes and with different abilities.
complete.values: Inclusive mobility and context-sensitive street design.
complete.limit: A section alone does not verify crossings, speeds, networks or accessibility compliance.

shared.label: Shared-street / woonerf principles
shared.meaning: Low-speed shared space that places pedestrian use and social activity at the centre.
shared.limit: Shared appearance without speed management and accessible navigation is insufficient.

active.label: Walking / cycling network priority
active.meaning: Providing connected, useful routes for walking and cycling.
active.values: Direct everyday access and alternatives to driving.
active.limit: A disconnected fragment does not establish a usable network.

child.label: Child-friendly / school-street principles
child.meaning: Designing daily routes and outdoor spaces around children’s access, play and comfort.
child.limit: Safety and accessibility need detailed design and operational checks.

auto.label: Automobile-oriented / road-hierarchy pattern
auto.meaning: Organising frontage, access or movement around motor vehicles and a hierarchy of roads.
auto.limit: This describes a spatial priority, not the political beliefs of designers or users.

modernist_plan.label: Modernist planning — possible comparison
modernist_plan.meaning: A comparison lens for freestanding slabs, separated circulation and large-scale composition.
modernist_plan.values: Discuss functional organisation and the relationship of buildings to open space.
modernist_plan.limit: Architectural Modernism and Modernist planning are different; a slab alone proves neither master-plan intent nor historical authorship.

biophilic.label: Biophilic design principles
biophilic.meaning: Strengthening people’s experience of nature through the built environment.
biophilic.limit: Visible greenery is an opportunity to discuss the principle, not proof of health or environmental outcomes.

landscape.label: Landscape-led / naturalistic public realm
landscape.meaning: Composing routes, views and activities around landscape character.
landscape.values: Restoration, outdoor experience and attention to the site.
landscape.limit: A park does not establish a complete landscape-urbanism philosophy or an Olmsted attribution.

neutral.label: Context-dependent / no specific ideology
neutral.meaning: The object can serve several kinds of neighbourhood or planning approach.
neutral.values: Ask how it is placed and connected.
neutral.limit: Use this explicitly rather than inventing a planning identity from an object’s appearance.

choices.legacy_variant_description: A contemporary timber sanctuary with a tall glazed front gable, eight exposed portal frames, warm timber walls and a low community annex. A level entrance leads to a broad centre aisle and two pew banks.

choices.legacy_variant_description: Converted machiya as cafe/gallery with original timber structure, earthen walls, open interior revealing garden, and hand-crafted interior furnishings.

Painted pale cream to imitate Venetian palazzo in stone. Elaborate projecting cornice with paired brackets. Originally housed a luxury housewares store with the first commercial Otis elevator.

choices.student_explanation: Rounded corners, smooth surfaces and strong horizontal bands.

source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Mies van der Rohe's iconic 1951 glass pavilion in Plano, Illinois. source_families.description: Traditional Dutch brown cafe (bruine kroeg), a centuries-old pub typology with dark wood-paneled interiors stained by generations of tobacco smoke. The exterior features a modest 1-2 storey brick or painted facade with frosted lower windows for privacy, a simple hanging sign, and often a corner entrance. These intimate establishments evolved from converted front rooms of private houses and remain neighborhood social anchors throughout Amsterdam.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Canal Warehouse
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Seventeenth-century Amsterdam canal warehouse (pakhuis), built during the Dutch Golden Age to store goods arriving by barge from the VOC and WIC trade routes. Massive thick-walled brick construction with large shuttered loading doors on every floor, a prominent hoisting beam (hijsbalk) projecting from the gable apex, and a utilitarian spout or step gable. These warehouses lined the Prinsengracht and Brouwersgracht, storing spices, coffee, grain, and textiles.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Cornice House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Neo-classical Amsterdam canal house with a horizontal cornice termination rather than a gable, representing the 18th-century shift toward French and Louis XVI-influenced architectural tastes. The facade features a symmetrical composition with decorative modillions, dentil moldings, and an elevated crown cornice that houses a hatchway for the hoisting beam. Flat-topped profile replaced earlier gable forms after 1790 as Amsterdam's architectural fashion evolved.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Hofje
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Traditional Dutch almshouse courtyard (hofje), a charitable housing typology dating to the 13th century where wealthy Amsterdam citizens built small houses arranged around a communal garden courtyard for elderly widows and the poor. Accessed through a single narrow passage from the street, the hofje creates a serene enclosed world hidden behind the busy canal-side facades. Most were built in the 17th century during the Golden Age, with the Begijnhof (14th century) being the most famous example.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Jordaan House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Working-class house from Amsterdam's Jordaan neighborhood, a planned residential district for laborers, craftsmen, and immigrants built during the 1612 city expansion. Narrow, modest brick facade (4-5m wide) with minimal ornamentation, small windows, and a simple gable form. The Jordaan's dense grid of narrow streets and small canals housed 85,000 people by the 1890s, making it one of the world's most densely populated zones. Many houses date to the 17th-18th century and have since been renovated as desirable inner-city housing.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Neck Gable House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The most ornate of Amsterdam's canal house gable types, the neck gable (halsgevel) was first designed by architect Philips Vingboons at Herengracht 168 in the mid-17th century. Features a decorative narrow neck connecting the facade wall to the gable top, flanked by elaborate scrollwork, pilasters, festoons, and pediments. The half-pilasters create an optical illusion of depth, making the already impressive facade appear even grander. This gable form became a characteristic hallmark of Amsterdam architecture that spread internationally.

source_families.title: Amsterdam School Housing
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Expressionist housing block from the Amsterdam School movement (1910-1930), characterized by sculptural brickwork, organic curved corners, elaborately patterned window arrangements, and richly handcrafted details. Designed by architects like Michel de Klerk and Piet Kramer, these social housing blocks were imbued with socialist ideals — bringing artistry and dignity to working-class housing. Het Schip (1920) by De Klerk is the masterpiece of the movement, featuring 102 apartments with sculptured facades, a corner tower, and integrated community facilities.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Spout Gable House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The earliest and simplest Amsterdam gable type, the spout gable (tuitgevel) dates from approximately 1620-1720. Features a restrained triangular gable profile with raised shoulders and a flat-topped rectangular spout at the apex resembling an inverted funnel. Originally common on warehouses along the Prinsengracht and islands like Uilenburg, the spout gable signified trade and storage rather than residential prestige. Semi-circular windows with wooden shutters are a characteristic feature.

source_families.title: Amsterdam Step Gable House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: One of Amsterdam's most iconic architectural forms, the step gable (trapgevel or crow-stepped gable) features a stairstep profile where the parapet wall rises above the roofline in a stepped pattern. Built primarily between 1600 and 1665 after Flemish immigrants replaced Amsterdam's timber facades with brick, the step gable was both decorative and practical — providing roof access and a convenient way to finish brick courses. Approximately one hundred original step-gable houses survive in Amsterdam today, symbolizing wealth and status during the Dutch Golden Age.

source_families.title: Barcelona Corner Chamfer
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The distinctive corner building of Barcelona's Eixample district, featuring the signature 45-degree chamfered corner (xamfra) mandated by Ildefons Cerda's 1859 urban plan. Each octagonal block in the grid measures 113m x 113m, with every corner cut at 45 degrees to improve visibility and accommodate the steam tram's turning radius. Typically 5-7 storeys with continuous iron balconies on every floor, ornamental stonework, and ground-floor commercial arcades. The chamfered corner often receives the building's most elaborate architectural treatment.

source_families.title: Barcelona Mercat
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Traditional Barcelona covered market hall (mercat), an essential neighborhood institution combining iron-and-glass industrial architecture with Modernista decorative exuberance. Barcelona's network of over 40 municipal markets dates from the 19th century, with the most iconic — like La Boqueria (1840/1914) and Mercat de Sant Antoni (1882) — featuring soaring iron and glass structures, colorful ceramic tile decoration, and wrought-iron cresting. The 1914 iron roof of La Boqueria, designed by Antoni de Falguera, crowned the market with polychrome stained-glass panels.

source_families.title: Barcelona Modernist Workshop
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Modernista industrial workshop or small factory from Barcelona's late 19th-century industrial boom, combining robust brick and iron construction with Art Nouveau decorative sensibilities. The Catalan industrial bourgeoisie built textile mills, ceramic workshops, and printing houses that showcased both engineering prowess and artistic ambition. Josep Puig i Cadafalch's Antiga Fabrica Casamarona (1911, now CaixaForum) exemplifies the style — Moorish-influenced brickwork with cast-iron pillars and steel beams, crowned by a distinctive sawtooth roof for north light.

source_families.title: Barcelona Townhouse
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Traditional Barcelona townhouse found throughout the city's older neighborhoods — Gothic Quarter, Gracia, Poblenou, and Barceloneta. Narrow 3-5 storey facade (6-8m wide) with continuous wrought-iron balconies on every floor, wooden slatted shutters (persianas), and ceramic tile decorative accents. Ground floor typically houses a shop or workshop, with residential floors above. The facade combines rendered masonry or stone with the characteristic Mediterranean vocabulary of iron balconies, shuttered French windows, and colorful tile.

source_families.title: Ecole Republicaine
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Third Republic-era school building (1880s-1900s) built during the Jules Ferry educational reforms. Symmetrical brick and stone institutional facade with carved 'ECOLE' inscription above entrance, separate boys' and girls' entrances flanking a central clock tower, tall arched windows for classroom daylight, and a hip roof with slate tiles. A civic monument to secular public education.

source_families.title: Eixample Apartment Block
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Barcelona Eixample apartment building within the Cerda grid. 5-7 floors of gallery-windowed facade with ornate iron balconies on every level, chamfered corner entries following the octagonal block geometry, interior courtyard (pati de llums), and a tribune gallery on the principal floor. Cream or ochre stucco with classical or Modernista ornament.

source_families.title: Grand Magasin
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Parisian grand department store in the Beaux-Arts tradition. Monumental 5-8 storey retail palace with ornate stone facade, grand glass dome or atrium at centre, Art Nouveau ironwork balconies and staircases, multiple boulevard entrances, and continuous display windows at street level. Inspired by Galeries Lafayette, Le Bon Marche, and Le Printemps.

source_families.title: Hotel Particulier
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Parisian private mansion (hotel particulier) arranged entre cour et jardin -- between a cobbled entrance court (cour d'honneur) and a private garden behind. 2-4 floors of restrained limestone elegance with a porte-cochere carriage entrance, rusticated ground floor, tall piano nobile windows, and a slate mansard roof. The quintessential aristocratic Parisian residence.

source_families.title: Marche Couvert
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: French covered market hall in the Baltard tradition. 1-2 floors of modular cast-iron and wrought-iron structural frame filled with glass and brick, creating a light-filled open-plan market interior. Prefabricated standardized metal components inspired by railway shed engineering, with natural daylight through glass roof panels and central nave clerestory.

source_families.title: Parisian Cafe Brasserie
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Traditional Parisian corner cafe or brasserie with zinc bar counter, Art Nouveau interior details, mirrored walls, mosaic tile floor, and wicker rattan terrace chairs under a canvas awning. Ornate painted lettering on fascia, bistro-height ground floor with residential above. The quintessential Parisian social institution.

source_families.title: Parisian Corner with Dome
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Haussmann corner building crowned with a decorative dome or cupola turret at the intersection angle. 6-8 floors of classic Haussmann limestone with enhanced ornament at this prominent location -- sculpted caryatids, wrought-iron balconies, and a zinc or copper dome rising above the mansard roofline. Typically sited at major boulevard intersections for maximum visual impact.

source_families.title: Passage Couvert
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Parisian covered shopping passage or arcade with glass-roofed pedestrian gallery lined with boutique shops. 2-3 floors of Neoclassical or Romantic-era facade lining a narrow glass-vaulted pedestrian way, decorative mosaic floors, ornate painted and carved ceiling panels, and gaslight-era atmosphere. Among the earliest commercial arcades in Europe.

source_families.title: Pre-Haussmann Marais Building
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Pre-Haussmann building from the medieval or Renaissance Marais district. 3-5 floors of irregular facade with exposed timber-frame (colombage) construction, narrow street frontage, steeply pitched roof with triangular pediment, and St. Andrew's cross timber patterns. Dates from 14th-17th century before Haussmann regularization, preserved in the protected Marais district.

source_families.title: Georgian Terrace House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Georgian terrace house (1714-1830) in London stock brick with strict symmetrical proportions. 3-4 floors with graduated sash windows (tallest on piano nobile, nearly square at top), semi-circular fanlight above six-panel front door, iron railings protecting basement area, and tuck-pointed brickwork in Flemish bond. The definitive London residential type.

source_families.title: London Crescent Terrace
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Curved crescent terrace following street geometry with a unified architectural facade spanning 30 or more houses. 3-5 floors of continuous elevation with Ionic columns, unified stone or stucco treatment, and a sweeping palatial effect designed to be read as a single grand composition rather than individual houses. Inspired by the Royal Crescent in Bath and Nash's London terraces.

source_families.title: London Mews House
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Converted London mews house, originally built as stables and carriage houses behind larger Georgian or Victorian residences. 2-3 floors on a cobbled no-through lane with arched carriage entrance (now garage or living space), intimate scale, no rear windows (to prevent servants spying on their employers' gardens), and a charming village-like atmosphere within central London.

source_families.title: London Heritage Mansion Block
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Late-Victorian London mansion block or commercial house with a finely carved Portland-stone facade, deep sash windows, a rusticated base, projecting pavilions, and a dormered slate mansard roof. The family is designed as a premium hero-building kit with strong base-body-crown hierarchy and readable architectural detail at street and aerial scales.

source_families.title: London Townhouse
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Georgian or Victorian London townhouse in brick, typically 3-5 floors with a narrow deep plan. Features include sash windows with stone or stucco dressings, iron railings at front area, portico entrance, and bay windows on Victorian examples. The standard London residential building type spanning 150 years of evolving taste from Georgian restraint to Victorian exuberance.

source_families.title: Regency Stucco Terrace
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Regency stucco terrace (1810-1840) in the John Nash style with brilliant white stucco facade, Ionic or Corinthian columns, wrought-iron balconies with canopy-style metal roofs, ornate entablature running the full terrace length, and a grand unified composition. Nash's Regent's Park terraces epitomize this type -- individual houses dressed as a single palace.

source_families.title: Victorian Bay Window Terrace
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Victorian bay-window terrace house (1850-1901) with projecting canted or square bay windows that became the defining feature of middle-class Victorian residential streets. 2-3 floors in red or yellow stock brick with decorative brickwork, slate roof, front garden with low brick wall and iron railings, and tiled front path. The most numerous London residential type.

source_families.title: New York Art Deco Tower
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: 1920s-1930s Art Deco office tower shaped by the 1916 Zoning Resolution's setback requirements. Sculptural stepped massing rises from a broad base through wedding-cake setbacks to an ornamental crown or spire. Facades clad in limestone and polychrome terra cotta with geometric zigzag, chevron, and sunburst motifs. Verticality emphasized by uninterrupted piers between spandrel panels. Elaborate lobby interiors with marble, bronze, and murals. Exemplified by the Chrysler Building, Empire State Building, and One Wall Street.

source_families.title: New York Corner Bodega
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Quintessential NYC corner bodega occupying the ground floor of a 4-5 storey tenement or mixed-use building. Characterized by bold hand-painted signage, corrugated metal awnings in yellow or green, corner entrance with angled door, stacked product displays spilling onto the sidewalk, neon beer signs, and a resident bodega cat. A vital neighborhood institution providing groceries, deli counter, coffee, and community connection on virtually every New York block.

source_families.title: New York Pre-War Apartment
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Grand pre-war apartment building from 1900-1940, the golden age of luxury Manhattan residential architecture. 6-15 floors in brick with limestone trim, featuring elaborate cornices, ornamental terra cotta, decorative water towers, and generous floor plans with formal rooms. Often designed by master architects like Emery Roth, Rosario Candela, and Schwartz & Gross. Concentrated on Central Park West, the Upper West Side, and Park Avenue. Landmark examples include the San Remo, the Beresford, and the Eldorado.

source_families.title: New York Walk-Up Tenement
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: New York walk-up tenement building from the 1860s-1920s, the dominant housing type of immigrant New York. 5-6 storey narrow brick buildings built under Old Law (1879) or New Law (1901) tenement regulations. Dumbbell-plan air shafts, ornate pressed-metal or stone cornices, cast-iron fire escapes, and elaborate Italianate or Queen Anne facade ornament belie the cramped interiors. The fire escape has become an iconic symbol of New York streetscape character.

source_families.title: SoHo Cast-Iron Loft Building
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: 1850s-1880s SoHo cast-iron facade loft building, part of the largest concentration of cast-iron architecture in the world. Prefabricated cast-iron facade columns and ornamental elements bolted together on-site, originally painted to imitate stone. Italianate or French Second Empire styling with Corinthian columns, round-arched windows, projecting cornices, and vast window openings that flood interiors with light. Originally commercial warehouses and light manufacturing, now converted to galleries, lofts, and retail.

source_families.title: Halifax Ferry Terminal
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Halifax harbour ferry terminal serving the oldest saltwater ferry service in North America (since 1752), connecting Halifax and Dartmouth across the harbour. A functional maritime transit building on the waterfront boardwalk with covered waiting areas, gangway access to vessels, and views across Halifax Harbour. The terminal sits within the revitalized waterfront precinct alongside Historic Properties and the boardwalk promenade.

source_families.title: Halifax Georgian Colonial
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Georgian colonial house from Halifax's founding era (1749-1830), representing the earliest built heritage of the city. Characterized by strict bilateral symmetry, a centered paneled front door with semicircular fanlight transom, 5-bay facade with regularly spaced double-hung sash windows, and construction in Maritime clapboard or wood shingle siding. Low hip or gable roof with wide chimneys at end walls. Influenced by British Georgian architectural pattern books adapted to Nova Scotia's harsh Maritime climate and locally available materials.

source_families.title: Halifax Maritime Commercial
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Maritime commercial building from Halifax's Historic Properties area on the waterfront, representing the most significant pre-Confederation complex of maritime commercial buildings in Canada. 2-4 storey stone or brick buildings constructed between 1800-1875 for merchants, trading and shipping companies. Heavy, unadorned construction with ironstone or granite walls, sandstone trim, functional warehouse character adapted for commerce. Associated with historic figures like privateer Enos Collins.

source_families.title: Halifax Painted Clapboard Row
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Colorful painted wood clapboard row housing characteristic of Halifax's North End, South End, and peninsula neighborhoods. 2-3 storey flat-fronted wooden houses snugged up to each other and the sidewalk, painted in vibrant Maritime colors — reds, blues, yellows, greens, and purples. Featuring gabled roofs, front porches, bay windows, and Victorian Gothic or Italianate trim details. The Four Sister Houses in the North End exemplify this distinctly Maritime housing type. Represents Halifax's 19th and early 20th century working-class and middle-class residential fabric.

source_families.title: Halifax Waterfront Warehouse
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Halifax waterfront warehouse from the 19th century — heavy stone or brick commercial warehouse buildings on the harbour, constructed for merchants and shipping companies between 1800-1875. Part of the nationally designated Halifax Waterfront Buildings historic site, the most significant pre-Confederation complex of maritime commercial buildings in Canada. Heavy timber frame construction with ironstone, granite, or brick walls, sandstone trim, loading doors at wharf level, and small window apertures in thick masonry walls.

source_families.title: Hydrostone Neighbourhood House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Distinctive Hydrostone neighbourhood house from the 1918-1920 reconstruction of Halifax's North End after the devastating 1917 Halifax Explosion. Built using Hydro-Stone — hydraulically-pressed concrete blocks with crushed granite aggregate finished to approximate the appearance of cut stone. Designed by architect George Ross and planned by town planner Thomas Adams in the English Garden City style, over 325 fireproof dwellings were constructed along tree-lined boulevards with a central public park. Designated a National Historic Site of Canada as one of the first planned housing projects in North America.

source_families.title: Inglewood Heritage Brick Commercial
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Heritage brick commercial building on 9th Avenue SE in Inglewood, Calgary's oldest neighbourhood. 2-3 storey Edwardian commercial buildings built between 1904-1914 during Calgary's pre-WWI boom, featuring red or buff brick construction with sandstone trim, decorative cornices, large commercial display windows at ground floor, and flat roofs behind ornamental parapets. 9th Avenue (originally Atlantic Avenue) was Calgary's first main street, established in the early 1880s. Many buildings retain original character while housing creative businesses, antique shops, and restaurants.

source_families.title: Modernisme Casa
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Catalan Modernisme (Art Nouveau) residential building from 1888-1911, the golden age of Barcelona's cultural and architectural renaissance. 3-5 storey residential buildings featuring organic curvilinear forms, ornate wrought-iron balconies, colorful ceramic tile (trencadis) cladding, carved stone facades with naturalistic motifs, and stained glass. Created by master architects Antoni Gaudi, Lluis Domenech i Montaner, and Josep Puig i Cadafalch along the Eixample's grid of chamfered blocks. Characterized by the predominance of curve over straight line, vegetal and organic ornamentation, and refined asymmetric aestheticism.

source_families.title: Calgary Beltline Mid-Rise
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Contemporary mid-rise condominium typical of Calgary's Beltline neighbourhood along 17th Avenue SW, built from the 2000s to 2020s. Four to eight storeys with active ground-floor retail, podium parking, and a mix of glass curtain wall, composite panel, and brick cladding. Flat roofs with rooftop amenity terraces are common, and the massing steps back at upper floors to respect the pedestrian scale of 17th Avenue's vibrant restaurant and boutique strip.

source_families.title: Calgary CTrain Station
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Light rail transit station for Calgary's CTrain system, the first modern LRT in North America, opened in 1981 for the Red Line. Stations range from utilitarian concrete platforms with steel-and-glass canopy shelters to distinctive community-designed structures like Brentwood's grain-elevator form. Platform-level boarding with low-floor access, windscreens for prairie weather protection, and Calgary Transit's signature red-and-white branding.

source_families.title: Calgary Inner-City Bungalow
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Calgary's pre-war inner-city bungalow found in neighbourhoods like Hillhurst, Sunnyside, Inglewood, and Mount Pleasant, built between 1910 and 1950. Typically one to one-and-a-half storeys with a full basement, wood-frame construction clad in painted clapboard or stucco, front porch with tapered columns, and a low-pitched gable or hip roof with exposed rafter tails. Many feature river-rock or clinker-brick fireplace chimneys, lead-glass windows, and old-growth fir flooring from Calgary's first building boom.

source_families.title: Calgary Modern Infill House
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Narrow-lot contemporary infill house replacing older bungalows in Calgary's inner-city neighbourhoods like Marda Loop, Altadore, and Bridgeland since the 2010s. Typically two to three storeys on a 25-foot-wide lot, featuring flat or shed roofs, clean geometric massing, and a mix of stucco, wood, and metal panel cladding. Creative solutions like central light courts, full-height stairwells, and clerestory glazing maximize natural light on tight sites. Detached rear garage or laneway suite accessed from the back alley.

source_families.title: Calgary New Central Library
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Calgary's New Central Library designed by Snohetta and DIALOG, opened November 2018. A 240,000 sq ft civic landmark featuring a dynamic triple-glazed hexagonal facade in fritted glass and iridescent aluminum panels that evoke open books and snowflakes. The crystalline envelope is carved away at street level to reveal an expansive double-curved western red cedar timber arch — one of the world's largest freeform timber shells — inspired by the Chinook cloud arches over the Rocky Mountain foothills. The building bridges over the CTrain Green Line tracks.

source_families.title: Calgary +15 Connected Tower
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Downtown Calgary office tower connected to the +15 skywalk system — the world's most extensive elevated pedestrian network with 16 kilometres of enclosed bridges linking 130 buildings at 15 feet above street level. Towers range from 1970s dark-glass and precast-concrete originals to contemporary glass curtain wall designs, all featuring +15 bridge connections that integrate with the building's atrium or lobby. The system allows year-round climate-controlled pedestrian movement through Calgary's downtown core.

source_families.title: Calgary Sandstone Heritage
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Paskapoo sandstone commercial building from Calgary's sandstone era (1886-1914), built after the great fire of 1886 prompted a shift from wood to stone construction. Two to four storeys in warm buff-yellow Paskapoo sandstone quarried from the Paleocene-era formations along the Bow and Elbow rivers. Romanesque Revival or Edwardian Classical detailing with rounded arches, rusticated stone base, corbelled cornices, and carved sandstone ornament. Many survive along Stephen Avenue, built by Scottish stonemasons who made Calgary the 'Sandstone City.'

source_families.title: Gastown Heritage Commercial
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Heritage commercial building from Vancouver's Gastown district, a National Historic Site containing 141 buildings built mostly between 1886 and 1914. Three to five storeys in brick and stone, constructed after the Great Fire of 1886 destroyed the original wood buildings. Victorian Italianate, Romanesque Revival, and Edwardian commercial styles with ornate cornices, corbelled brickwork, cast-iron columns, and decorative window pediments. The continuous streetwall of varied facade treatments creates one of Vancouver's most distinctive urban districts.

source_families.title: Vancouver Craftsman Bungalow
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: West Coast Craftsman bungalow built between 1910 and 1930, found throughout Kitsilano, Mount Pleasant, Grandview-Woodland, and East Vancouver. One to one-and-a-half storeys with a low-pitched gable roof, deep overhanging eaves with exposed rafter tails, and a prominent integral front porch supported by thick tapered columns on clinker-brick or river-rock piers. Exteriors clad in cedar shingles or clapboard, with decorative triangular knee brackets under gable eaves and divided-light windows. Vancouver's version shows Pacific Northwest influences including cedar materials and sometimes mock-Japanese carved fascia details.

source_families.title: Vancouver Laneway House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Detached accessory dwelling unit built at the rear of single-family lots along Vancouver's back lanes, legalized by the city's 2009 zoning bylaw. One to one-and-a-half storeys (maximum 8.5 metres height), typically 500-1,000 square feet on a compact footprint above or beside a single-car garage. Over 7,000 have been built since 2009, representing a key form of 'gentle densification' and missing-middle housing. Designs range from contemporary flat-roof boxes to gabled forms harmonizing with the main house character.

source_families.title: Vancouver Special
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The only house style unique to Greater Vancouver, built by the thousands between 1965 and 1985. A front-gabled two-storey box built on grade with a very shallow-pitched roof, designed to maximize square footage on narrow 33-foot lots by exploiting a zoning loophole that excluded basements from floor area calculations. Characterized by a distinctive shallow upper balcony with iron or aluminum railings, decorative brick on the ground-floor front facade with stucco above, and a front door set to one side for easy up-down duplex conversion. The city changed its building code in 1985 to prevent further construction of this style.

source_families.title: Vancouverism Tower-Podium
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The signature building typology of 'Vancouverism' — a slender residential point tower rising from a low-rise townhouse or retail podium that defines the street edge. Developed from the 1990s onward, this urban design model combines New York brownstone-inspired podiums with Hong Kong-inspired slim towers to preserve views, maximize density, and maintain street-level vibrancy. Podiums typically 3-6 storeys with townhouse units, retail, and amenity space, while towers above are slender enough (typically under 20m floor plate width) to allow light and views between buildings.

source_families.title: SkyTrain Elevated Station
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Elevated rapid transit station for Vancouver's SkyTrain automated light metro system, opened in 1985 for Expo 86. Stations are elevated on concrete guideway with platform canopies and enclosed fare-paid zones. Original Expo Line stations designed by Austrian firm Habegger and Vancouver's Allen Parker & Associates feature distinctive rounded structural forms and hoop-truss architecture. Newer Millennium Line stations include award-winning designs like Brentwood's double-curved timber canopy resembling a canoe. Canada Line stations use sleek glass-and-steel modernist language.

source_families.title: West End Mid-Century Tower
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Concrete modernist apartment tower from Vancouver's West End, built during the massive rezoning and construction boom of the 1960s and early 1970s that transformed the neighbourhood from single-family houses to one of North America's densest residential areas. Ten to twenty storeys in reinforced concrete with expressed structural frames, sculptural balcony forms, and breezeway details. Architects like Rix Reinecke designed buildings like Ocean Towers (1958) that use balcony shapes as sculptural elements referencing the nearby English Bay waterfront. The West End west of Denman Street has one of Vancouver's largest concentrations of mid-century residential architecture.

source_families.title: Annex Mansion
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Grand detached mansion from Toronto's Annex neighbourhood built 1880s-1900s for the city's wealthiest families. Features Richardsonian Romanesque arches in Credit Valley sandstone with Queen Anne turrets and decorative terra cotta, designed by architects like E.J. Lennox. Rich red brick and plum-pink sandstone facades with pyramidal roofs, spindled wooden porches, and recessed grand archways.

source_families.title: Bay-and-Gable House
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Toronto's signature residential form built 1875-1900, combining Italianate and Gothic Revival elements. Features a large projecting bay window covering more than half the front facade surmounted by a steeply pitched decorated gable with ornate bargeboard trim. Built in red or yellow Don Valley brick with polychromatic detailing, stained glass transoms, and tall windows with low sills for maximum light.

source_families.title: Brick Rowhouse Terrace
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Continuous brick rowhouse terrace typifying Toronto's Cabbagetown and Riverdale neighbourhoods, built during the 1880s building boom. Features polychromatic brickwork in High Victorian Gothic style, bay-and-gable fronts in repeated rhythm, corbelled brick cornices, and narrow lots driven by frontage-based property taxes. Often semi-detached pairs or continuous runs of 6-12 units forming a strong streetwall.

source_families.title: Condo Podium Tower
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Toronto's defining contemporary residential typology: a slender glass point tower rising 20-60 storeys above a 3-6 storey podium containing retail, lobby, and amenities. Characterized by undulating glass balconies, curtain wall facades, and a podium that addresses the streetwall while the tower steps back to reduce wind impacts. Exemplified by towers along the waterfront, Yonge corridor, and CityPlace.

source_families.title: Edwardian Foursquare
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Boxy practical house built 1900-1920 across Toronto's streetcar suburbs including High Park, Riverdale, Roncesvalles, and the Beaches. Named for its four-square-room-per-floor plan with a pyramidal hip roof, front dormer, and generous full-width front porch with classical columns. A reaction against Victorian ornamental excess, featuring simpler detailing with solid front doors, restrained stained glass, and broader footprints than earlier Victorian houses.

source_families.title: Junction Converted Industrial Loft
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Former factory or warehouse in Toronto's Junction neighbourhood converted to residential lofts and creative studios. Built early 1900s for manufacturing, featuring heavy timber and steel structure, exposed brick walls, high ceilings of 3.5-8 metres, large industrial windows, and cast-iron columns. Adaptive reuse retains original character while inserting contemporary living spaces, often with Crittall-style steel windows and new rooftop additions.

source_families.title: TTC Streetcar Platform Stop
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Street-median transit stop serving Toronto's TTC streetcar network, the largest in North America. Features raised concrete platform in the road median with accessible ramps, heated shelters with curved glass canopies, fare equipment, and real-time arrival displays. Modern designs include widened sidewalk bumpout stops as on rebuilt Roncesvalles Avenue. The stop creates a civic presence on the street median with distinctive TTC red branding.

source_families.title: Mile End Cultural Triplex
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Montreal Mile End triplex with ground-floor cultural or commercial use and two residential floors above, connected by signature exterior iron staircases. Built during Montreal's 1900-1920 expansion, these plexes feature brick facades with ornamental cornices, wrought-iron spiral or L-shaped staircases with floral scrollwork, and flat roofs. The ground floor hosts cafes, galleries, or bookshops that define Mile End's creative neighbourhood identity.

source_families.title: Corner Dépanneur
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Iconic Montreal corner convenience store (dépanneur) typically occupying the ground floor of a residential building at a street intersection. Features distinctive vintage signage, often with Coca-Cola or beer brand branding, corner entrance with angled door, tin or retractable awnings, and residential apartments above. Built from the 1890s onwards, the dépanneur is a social anchor of Montreal's working-class neighbourhoods, with brick or stone construction and painted commercial facades.

source_families.title: Montreal Duplex
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Classic Montreal duplex with one apartment per floor, built during the great expansion of 1900-1920. Defined by its external iron staircase providing separate entrances for the upper and lower units, shared balcony landings, and flat roof. Brick construction with ornamental cornices, tall windows, and the distinctive Montreal plex form that allows upstairs tenants a separate entrance from the downstairs, originally inspired by older Quebec duplex traditions.

source_families.title: Montreal Plateau Triplex
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Montreal's most iconic residential typology: the Plateau triplex with three stacked apartments accessed by ornamental wrought-iron exterior spiral staircases. Built 1870-1930 during the city's industrial expansion, these plexes feature brick facades with elaborate pressed-tin or carved wood cornices, decorative iron scrollwork with loops, leaves, and floral motifs, and flat roofs. The exterior staircase was mandated by narrow lot frontages and became the defining symbol of Montreal's residential streetscape.

source_families.title: Second Empire Civic Building
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Monumental civic building in the Second Empire style exemplified by Montreal City Hall (Hôtel de Ville, 1872-1878) designed by Perrault and Hutchison. Features the signature mansard roof with ornate dormer windows, grey limestone facades with turrets and balconies, symmetrical composition, and a central clock tower. Rough-faced stone construction with ashlar trim, iron cresting on the mansard ridge, and tripartite dormer windows piercing the steep slate roof slopes.

source_families.title: Old Montreal Limestone Commercial
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Grey limestone commercial building from Old Montreal's historic core, dating from the French Colonial era through Victorian expansion (1700s-1870s). Thick stone walls originally built for fire protection and cold insulation, featuring arcade ground floors, rusticated stone bases, and Victorian eclectic upper-floor detailing. Found along Rue Saint-Paul and Rue Sainte-Hélène where ten magnificently preserved store-and-warehouse buildings from 1858-1871 define the streetscape.

source_families.title: Old Montreal Warehouse Loft
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Massive warehouse or industrial building from Old Montreal's port and commercial district, built 1860s-1920s for grain storage, textile manufacturing, or port operations. Features thick load-bearing limestone or brick walls, heavy timber framing with exposed wood joists, cast-iron columns with decorative capitals, and large industrial openings. Now converted to residential lofts with soaring ceilings, exposed brick and timber, and contemporary insertions preserving the raw industrial character.

source_families.title: Administrative Faculty Office Building
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: A mid-rise administrative or faculty office building found on university and institutional campuses. 4-6 storeys of departmental offices, faculty workspaces, seminar rooms, and common meeting areas arranged on a corner or mid-block infill site with a pedestrian-friendly ground-floor lobby. Typically clad in a warm mix of brick masonry and contemporary metal, glass, or timber, expressing institutional permanence while hosting contemporary academic work.

source_families.title: Airport Terminal Building
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Airport terminal buildings are large-span civic infrastructure typologies that combine passenger processing, retail concessions, and gate access under dramatic roof structures. Their architectural character is defined by the tension between engineering spectacle — expressed trusses, vaulted canopies, cable-stayed masts — and the efficient movement of thousands of people per hour. Facades tend toward transparency at the landside frontage, with glazed curtain walls or arched fenestration inviting natural light into departure halls. Scale ranges from compact regional terminals to multi-gate complexes, each variant distinguished by structural language, era, and material philosophy. The building type consistently prioritizes civic legibility: a recognizable silhouette, generous canopy overhangs at drop-off, and a strong street presence that signals arrival.

source_families.title: Annex Mansion
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Annex Mansion is a grand late-Victorian detached residence characteristic of Toronto's Annex neighbourhood, built predominantly between the 1880s and 1910s for upper-middle-class and professional families. These large, freestanding homes are distinguished by their Richardsonian Romanesque or Queen Anne massing, featuring corner turrets, steeply pitched multi-gabled roofs, elaborate carved stone or brick ornamentation, and generous wrap-around verandahs. Facades typically combine rusticated sandstone or rock-faced granite with polychrome brick, creating richly textured streetscapes that sit close to the sidewalk behind low iron fencing. The program historically centred on a single grand household but many examples have since been converted to multi-unit dwellings or professional offices while retaining their architectural character. As landmark presences on residential streets, Annex Mansions anchor neighbourhood identity and set a high bar for heritage-sensitive infill and renovation.

source_families.title: Aquatic Natatorium Complex
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The aquatic natatorium complex is a large-span civic building type purpose-built to enclose Olympic or competition-grade swimming pools, leisure pools, and hydrotherapy facilities under a single expansive roof structure. The typology demands exceptional interior volume — typically 10–18 m clear height over pool halls — achieved through arched, vaulted, or cable-tensioned structural systems that also provide natural daylighting. Architecturally, natatoriums span a wide range of expression, from parametric sculptural shells in polycarbonate and tensioned steel to heritage Beaux-Arts bath-houses with cast-iron and glass barrel vaults, biophilic mass-timber arches with living roofs, and functional community recreation centres in profiled metal cladding. The building type sits at the intersection of civic infrastructure and public wellness, often serving as a landmark sports destination or neighbourhood health hub. Facades are characterised by large expanses of glazing to animate pool interiors and mediate condensation and humidity loads.

source_families.title: Bay and Gable House
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Bay and Gable House is a quintessential Victorian-era urban residential typology found predominantly in late-19th-century Canadian and American cities, characterized by a projecting front bay window rising one or two storeys and crowned by a decorative gabled dormer. The form combines Italianate massing with Gothic Revival ornamental detailing — scroll-cut bargeboards, finials, polychrome brick banding, and arched window surrounds — producing a richly articulated street presence on a compact semi-detached or detached lot. Facades typically employ load-bearing brick construction in buff, red, or cream tones, with contrasting brick voussoirs, stone sills, and painted wood trim providing rhythmic colour contrast. The typology sits flush or near-flush to the sidewalk, contributing to continuous streetwall definition in older inner-city neighbourhoods. As a duplex form it often accommodates two stacked residential units behind an architecturally unified Victorian frontage.

source_families.title: Biophilic Modern Healthcare
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Biophilic Modern Healthcare facilities integrate nature-forward design principles with clinical and wellness programming, prioritising patient wellbeing through direct exposure to greenery, natural light, and organic materials. These buildings weave living walls, rooftop gardens, and timber structural systems into their architectural language, creating environments that measurably reduce stress and accelerate recovery. The typology spans from compact urban clinics and community health centres to mid-rise specialist hospitals and wellness campuses, each grounded in a commitment to low-carbon construction and renewable energy integration. Facades are treated as ecological surfaces — solar panels, vertical gardens, timber louvres, and carved stone work in concert to blur the boundary between built form and landscape. The result is an institutional building type that reads as simultaneously calming and technologically progressive.

source_families.title: Boutique Hotel
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The boutique hotel typology encompasses intimate, design-forward lodging properties that prioritize distinct architectural identity over standardized hospitality formats. Typically occupying 20–80 rooms across 3–20 storeys, these buildings express strong curatorial intent through materials, massing, and street presence. Programs combine guest rooms with curated food-and-beverage, rooftop amenities, and activated ground-floor lobbies that engage the public realm. Architectural character ranges from adaptive reuse of historic fabric to purpose-built contemporary statements, unified by an emphasis on experiential arrival sequences and high-craft detailing. The typology thrives across urban neighborhoods, resort towns, and waterfront districts, anchoring its surroundings with a sense of place-specificity.

source_families.title: Brick Rowhouse Terrace
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The brick rowhouse terrace is a quintessential urban residential typology characterized by attached or semi-detached dwellings sharing party walls along a continuous street frontage. Rooted in Victorian and Edwardian building traditions, these terraces combine load-bearing red or dark-brown brick construction with decorative stone dressings, ornamental gabled rooflines, and rhythmically repeating window bays. The typology spans from highly ornamented Gothic Revival and Queen Anne terraces to plainer Edwardian semi-detached pairs and contemporary infill rowhouses with rooftop additions. Street presence is defined by low iron railings or hedged front gardens that maintain a clear threshold between public pavement and private entry. The archetype is well suited to inner-suburban and urban residential streets, delivering medium-density housing with strong neighbourhood character and heritage appeal.

source_families.title: Calgary 15 Connected Tower
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Calgary 15 Connected Tower is a mid-rise to high-rise office typology defined by its integration with Calgary's iconic +15 elevated pedestrian skywalk network, which links buildings at the second-floor level across downtown. These structures typically occupy full urban blocks or prominent corner sites, presenting assertive street-level podiums that connect directly to the enclosed walkway bridges. The archetype encompasses a spectrum from 1970s–80s brutalist-inflected concrete office slabs to contemporary curtain-wall towers with mixed-use podiums, all sharing the defining covered bridge connector as a civic and commercial amenity. Program typically includes ground-floor retail or lobby, office floors above, and in newer iterations, residential or hospitality uses in upper tower segments. The connected-tower typology is emblematic of Calgary's downtown urban form and cold-climate design culture.

source_families.title: Campus Dining Hall Food Court
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Campus dining halls and food courts serve as the social heart of university campuses, combining high-volume food service with flexible gathering space for students, faculty, and staff. These mid-rise civic buildings typically occupy prominent corner or quad-facing sites, employing a hybrid program of servery kitchen, multi-station food court, and open dining floors with generous daylighting. Architecturally, they balance institutional durability — load-bearing brick, concrete structure — with inviting transparency through large curtain-wall glazing that animates the street edge and signals public life within. Upper-level seating with terrace or mezzanine access, visible from the exterior, reinforces the communal character. Contemporary campus dining facilities often integrate sustainable features such as green roofs, warm wood cladding, and bicycle infrastructure to reflect campus sustainability goals.

source_families.title: Campus Lecture Hall Complex
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The campus lecture hall complex is a purpose-built institutional education facility housing large-capacity tiered auditoria, seminar rooms, and student gathering spaces. These buildings serve as intellectual and social anchors on university campuses, ranging from intimate mass-timber pavilions to monumental brutalist blocks and expressive parametric structures.
