Architecturally they are distinguished by their bold civic presence, generous entrance lobbies, and the architectural challenge of expressing large-volume interior spaces — raked seating floors, acoustic enclosures, and service cores — on the exterior. The typology spans mid-century concrete monumentalism, contemporary biophilic timber construction, sculptural parametric forms, and organic vernacular-inspired designs, each reflecting different eras and institutional cultures of higher education.

source_families.title: Campus Parking Structure
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Campus parking structures are multi-storey vehicle storage facilities designed to integrate with educational campuses and urban institutional contexts. These structures balance functional efficiency — long-span open decks, ramped circulation, and high-throughput entry/exit lanes — with contextual architectural expression that responds to adjacent campus buildings. Facades are typically screened or articulated to mask the utilitarian interior while presenting a civic face to the street, using materials such as brick, precast concrete panels, and metal louver screens. Corner stair towers, glazed elevator lobbies, and ground-floor retail or pedestrian-active frontages are common devices for urban compatibility. Floor-to-floor heights are taller than typical office construction to accommodate vehicle clearance, resulting in compact but visually substantial massing at 4–6 storeys.

source_families.title: Campus Recreation Athletics Centre
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A campus recreation and athletics centre is a mid-rise institutional facility anchoring student life through sport, fitness, and wellness programming. These buildings typically house gymnasiums, aquatic facilities, climbing walls, fitness floors, and multipurpose courts within large-footprint volumes articulated by tall curtain-wall glazing that reveals interior activity to the street. The typology bridges campus identity and civic presence, combining durable masonry or brick envelopes with expressive glass volumes that signal transparency and energy. Facades often integrate wood, concrete, and steel accents to balance institutional solidity with contemporary warmth. Street-level frontages prioritize pedestrian access with canopied entries, bike parking, and landscaped setbacks that animate the campus edge.

source_families.title: Central Utilities Plant Energy Centre
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: A central utilities plant or energy centre is a purpose-built urban infrastructure building housing mechanical and electrical plant — boilers, chillers, cooling towers, heat exchangers, and switchgear — that serves a district, campus, or dense mixed-use precinct. Architecturally, these buildings must reconcile heavy industrial servicing requirements (large ductwork penetrations, rooftop mechanical equipment, ventilation louvers) with urban-context sensitivity, resulting in facades that blend exposed structural honesty with masonry or cladding treatments. The typology ranges from compact 2–3 storey infill plant rooms set flush to the street grid, to taller 4–5 storey anchor buildings with expressed mechanical penthouses and glazed curtain-wall faces that reveal the machinery within. Common to all variants is the presence of visible infrastructure elements — exhaust stacks, cooling tower banks, large louver arrays, and surface-mounted pipework — treated as architectural features rather than afterthoughts.

source_families.title: Chateauesque Grand Railway Hotel
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The Chateauesque Grand Railway Hotel is a monumental late-Victorian hospitality typology conceived at the height of transcontinental railway expansion, when competing rail companies commissioned castle-like flagship hotels to anchor urban termini and mountain resort towns. Drawing on French Renaissance château forms filtered through Scottish baronial and Gothic Revival influences, these buildings are characterized by asymmetric massing, conical tourelles, steeply pitched slate roofs, and lavish stone carving that projected civic grandeur and national ambition. Programs typically encompass grand ballrooms, formal dining rooms, and several hundred guest rooms arranged along double-loaded corridors within a U- or L-shaped perimeter block. The street presence is deliberately theatrical — crenellated parapets, heraldic stone reliefs, and arched porte-cochères signal arrival and ceremony to guests approaching from street level. Across its four historical variants the typology ranges from raw-granite Scottish-baronial towers to cream Beaux-Arts limestone blocks, High Victorian Gothic limestone halls, and Alpine chalet-influenced resort wings.

source_families.title: Collegiate Gothic
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Collegiate Gothic is a historicist architectural tradition rooted in the medieval universities of Oxford and Cambridge, adapted across Britain and North America for academic, administrative, and ceremonial institutional buildings. The typology is defined by load-bearing stone or brick masonry, pointed Gothic arches, elaborate tracery windows, crenellated parapets, and vertical towers that signal institutional permanence and scholarly authority. Buildings are typically arranged around quadrangles or set as freestanding civic monuments along urban streets, with richly articulated facades that combine heraldic stonework, oriel windows, and decorative finials. The program encompasses lecture halls, libraries, collegiate common rooms, and administrative suites, often within a single monumental block. Rendered in warm limestone, red brick, or polychrome masonry, the aesthetic conveys learned tradition, civic gravitas, and aspirational heritage.

source_families.title: Condo Podium Tower
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The condo podium tower is a mixed-use residential high-rise typology defined by a distinct two-part massing: a street-activating podium base of 2–4 storeys housing retail or amenity programs, topped by a slender residential tower. This form mediates between the pedestrian scale of the street and the vertical ambition of urban density, making it a cornerstone of contemporary North American urban infill. Facades range from contextual red-brick podiums with glass curtain-wall towers to parametric curved forms and heritage retrofit bases, reflecting a broad stylistic spectrum. Balconies, expressed floor plates, and generous glazing are consistent tower characteristics regardless of variant. The typology typically delivers 80–300+ units per building, serving mid- to high-density residential growth in established urban neighbourhoods.

source_families.title: Contemporary Midrise
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Contemporary midrise residential buildings represent the dominant infill typology in urban neighborhoods undergoing densification, typically occupying narrow lots between 15–30 m wide and rising 5–9 storeys above street level. These buildings balance unit efficiency with architectural ambition, featuring articulated facades, integrated balconies, and high glazing ratios that animate the street edge. Programs typically include ground-floor residential lobbies or retail, stacked market-rate or mixed-income apartments, and rooftop amenity space. The typology spans a wide stylistic range — from warm mass-timber and biophilic curtain-wall expressions to crisp European white-render volumes and contextual brick compositions — allowing it to fit within both heritage streetscapes and emerging contemporary corridors. Quality of facade articulation, material warmth, and planting integration increasingly define the premium tier of this building type.

source_families.title: Convention Exhibition Center
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Convention and exhibition centers are large-span civic structures designed to host trade shows, conferences, public events, and cultural gatherings at an urban or regional scale. They typically feature column-free exhibition halls, flexible pre-function lobbies, and prominent civic frontages that signal public welcome. Architecturally the typology ranges from dramatic tensile and glass high-tech enclosures to biophilic mass-timber pavilions, parametric blob-form facades, and adaptive reuse of industrial heritage buildings. Their large footprints demand strong street-level engagement through canopies, glazed lobbies, and generous plazas that mediate between the megastructure and the pedestrian realm. The building form is driven by interior clear-span requirements, resulting in bold roof expressions — tensile membranes, sawtooth skylights, green roofs, or undulating composite panels — that become civic landmarks.

source_families.title: Corner Dépanneur
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The corner dépanneur is a quintessentially Québécois urban typology — a small-format convenience store occupying a chamfered or angled street corner lot, typically embedded within a residential neighbourhood fabric. Ranging from single-storey post-war vernacular to two-storey mixed-use blocks with a dwelling above the shop, these buildings anchor pedestrian life at intersections and serve as informal community landmarks. Architecturally modest and highly legible, they are defined by large display windows, hand-painted or mounted signage advertising lotto, bière froide, and cigarettes, and façades that accumulate decades of commercial ephemera. The typology spans eras from weathered mid-century stucco-over-brick to Art Deco corner blocks to tidy post-war red-brick mixed-use, and increasingly to renovated contemporary infill retaining the brick shell while updating the ground-floor retail expression.

source_families.title: Corporate Office Campus Headquarters
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The Corporate Office Campus Headquarters archetype encompasses purpose-built office environments designed to project institutional authority, brand identity, and organizational scale. These buildings range from sleek contemporary curtain-wall rotundas to neoclassical civic-scaled headquarters, biophilic mass-timber campuses, and adaptive industrial loft conversions. Program typically includes executive suites, collaborative workspaces, ground-floor reception lobbies, and landscaped public forecourts. Architectural character shifts dramatically across the typology spectrum — from the sculptural and formal to the raw and industrial — reflecting the diverse aesthetic philosophies of modern corporate culture. Each variant anchors a distinct urban or campus context, from downtown street corners to repurposed warehouse districts.

source_families.title: Cruise Ferry Terminal
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Cruise and ferry terminals are large-span waterfront civic buildings that serve as gateways between land and sea, combining ticketing, customs, passenger processing, and retail into a single monumental hall. The typology ranges from expressive contemporary structures with sculpted rooflines to beaux-arts civic monuments inherited from the golden age of ocean travel, and from sustainable mass-timber pavilions to utilitarian steel-clad operational sheds. Their principal architectural challenge is spanning vast interior volumes to accommodate passenger flows while creating a legible public face toward the city and an operational berth interface toward the water. Facades are typically horizontal and low-to-mid-rise, with emphasis on roof expression rather than vertical height. The building acts simultaneously as an urban landmark, a logistical machine, and a threshold experience announcing arrival or departure.

source_families.title: E Commerce Fulfillment Center
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: E-commerce fulfillment centers are large-footprint, logistics-intensive industrial buildings designed to receive, sort, store, and dispatch consumer goods at high velocity. The typology spans from heritage brick warehouses retrofitted with modern operations to purpose-built mega-sheds with automated racking systems, and increasingly encompasses sustainable formats featuring mass-timber structure, living roofs, and solar arrays. Architecturally, the program demands wide column-free floor plates, abundant dock-door bays along one or more facades, and ancillary office or mezzanine volumes that read as distinct elements against the main shed. The building's scale and repetitive dock-door rhythm define its street character, while sustainability mandates are pushing roofscape treatments — solar PV, sedum, and green corridors — into prominent design features.

source_families.title: Early 20th Century Megastructure
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Early 20th century industrial megastructures represent the monumental factory and rail-infrastructure buildings of the 1900–1940 period, characterized by vast single-storey or low-rise volumes designed to shelter large-span manufacturing, assembly, or logistics operations. These buildings pioneered the combination of load-bearing brick perimeter walls with exposed steel or timber truss roof systems, clerestory and sawtooth glazing for daylighting deep floor plates, and heavy concrete base courses capable of receiving rail spurs and heavy freight. Their architectural character oscillates between raw utilitarian pragmatism and a restrained industrial classicism, with regularly spaced pilasters, corbelled brick cornices, and rhythmic multi-pane steel-sash windows conferring a monumental dignity to production at scale. Today these structures are prized for adaptive reuse as creative offices, event halls, and cultural venues, their exposed structural skeletons and patinated materiality conveying an authenticity that contemporary construction cannot replicate.

source_families.title: Edwardian Foursquare
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Edwardian Foursquare is a quintessentially North American residential typology from the 1900s–1915 era, characterized by its boxy, nearly cubic two-storey massing, hipped or pyramidal roof, and full-width front porch. The plan is organized around a central stair with four rooms per floor — the origin of the 'foursquare' name — yielding efficient, symmetrical facades with regularly spaced double-hung windows. Architectural character ranges from austere red-brick vernacular to stucco-and-half-timber Arts-and-Crafts hybrids, natural stone Craftsman variants, and adaptive-reuse conversions with contemporary additions. The type dominates mature urban residential neighbourhoods across Canada and the American Midwest, typically set on modest lots with shallow front yards and prominent porch stoops. Its enduring appeal lies in the combination of generous interior volume, straightforward construction, and a civic street presence anchored by the deep covered porch.

source_families.title: Ev Charging Hub Mobility Station
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The EV Charging Hub & Mobility Station is a purpose-built urban infrastructure typology that combines fast-charging forecourts for electric vehicles with activated ground-floor amenities — cafés, waiting lounges, and micro-retail — to transform the utilitarian act of charging into a dwell-worthy public destination. Each hub integrates a prominent canopy or shade structure over the charging bays, supported by a compact service building of 1–2 storeys housing passenger amenities and energy management systems. The typology draws on sustainable design languages ranging from solar-integrated steel canopies to living green walls and mass-timber structures, signalling clean energy values through architectural expression. Sites are typically corner or mid-block urban infill plots with direct street frontage, generous forecourt paving, and landscape buffers that humanise the car-dominant programme. As EV adoption accelerates, these hubs function as the 21st-century successor to the petrol station, recast as civic-minded, pedestrian-friendly mobility nodes.

source_families.title: Glass Tower Modern
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The dominant form of contemporary urban office development: a full-curtain-wall tower rising from a distinguished podium base, delivering large floor-plate commercial space to dense downtown cores. The typology ranges from rectilinear corporate slabs in reflective blue or dark tinted glass to parametric sculpted towers with undulating balcony spandrels and integrated sky gardens. Ground-floor lobbies are expressed as transparent, double-height volumes with premium stone or structural-glass entries that activate the street edge, while facades emphasize vertical continuity with aluminum mullion grids, reflective glazing, and occasional setback crowns or spire elements marking the skyline.

source_families.title: Graduate Family Housing
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Graduate family housing provides subsidized residential accommodation for postgraduate students with dependents, typically developed and managed by universities on or adjacent to their campuses. These mid-rise buildings balance the density demands of urban university districts with the domestic scale and amenity requirements of family living — larger units, shared laundry, play areas, and community rooms. Architecturally they occupy a transitional character between institutional and residential, often clad in collegiate brick with contemporary detailing to signal both permanence and livability. Corner conditions and glazed stair towers are common compositional devices, and ground-floor activation through retail or community uses supports campus life. Sustainability features such as solar panels and balconies are increasingly standard in newer developments.

source_families.title: High Tech Structural Arena
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The High Tech Structural Arena is a large-span civic sports and entertainment venue defined by expressive structural systems that are as visually legible as they are performative. These buildings celebrate engineering honesty — cable nets, exposed steel trusses, geodesic skins, and tensile canopies are worn as architectural identity rather than concealed. Programs typically include multi-purpose bowl seating, concourse retail, hospitality clubs, and flexible event floors suitable for concerts, sport, and exhibitions. The typology spans from mid-century tensile pioneers to contemporary parametric envelopes, always prioritising span, drama, and urban presence. Street-facing facades are animated by structural expression, large glazed concourses, and landmark rooflines visible from city approaches.

source_families.title: Intermodal Transit Hub
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The intermodal transit hub is a large-footprint civic infrastructure building that consolidates rail, bus, metro, and active-transport modes under one roof, acting as a gateway node in the urban mobility network. Architecturally it is defined by its signature long-span roof structure — whether a sculptural steel exoskeleton, a monumental Beaux-Arts trainshed, a mass-timber arch hall, or a utilitarian steel-frame shed — that shelters vast concourse volumes and passenger circulation. The building typically presents a strong civic frontage to the street with generous glazed bays, covered drop-off canopies, and direct pedestrian connections to the public realm. Program includes ticketing halls, waiting concourses, retail and food-and-beverage, platform shelters, and back-of-house operations. Its scale and visibility make it a landmark within its district, with architectural ambition calibrated to the era and budget of the transit authority.

source_families.title: Junction Converted Industrial Loft
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Junction Converted Industrial Loft typology transforms early-twentieth-century factory and warehouse buildings into mixed-use live-work, creative-office, and retail destinations. Original heavy-timber or steel structural frames are preserved behind deep-red or buff brick envelopes punctuated by large multi-pane steel-framed windows that once lit factory floors. Adaptive reuse interventions range from sympathetic restoration of arched ground-floor openings and exposed wood trusses to contemporary rooftop glazed additions and green roofs. The buildings sit hard to the sidewalk in tight urban grain, activating street edges with generous ground-floor glazing and retained industrial character. Character details such as ghost signage, reclaimed brick, and expressed concrete banding distinguish this typology from new-build industrial pastiche.

source_families.title: Large Art Museum Gallery
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Large art museum galleries are major civic anchor institutions housing permanent collections, touring exhibitions, and public programming across expansive floor plates. The typology spans an extraordinary range of architectural expression — from Beaux-Arts neoclassical palaces to parametric deconstructivist sculptures, from biophilic earth-sheltered pavilions to adaptive-reuse industrial conversions. Programmatically, they demand column-free gallery halls, controlled-light exhibition rooms, grand public atria, loading docks, conservation labs, and generous civic forecourts. Their civic presence commands prominent urban sites, waterfront locations, or cultural campuses, and their architecture is frequently treated as a statement of civic identity and cultural ambition. Scale is invariably large, with floor plates exceeding 2,000 sqm and heights ranging from low-profile earth-integrated pavilions to multi-storey monumental institutions.

source_families.title: Mid Century Distribution Warehouse
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The mid-century distribution warehouse is a low-rise utilitarian building type developed primarily from the 1940s through 1970s to serve urban freight, wholesale, and light manufacturing networks. Characterised by deep floor plates, minimal fenestration, and a street-facing loading dock rhythm, these structures prioritise operational efficiency over architectural expression. Facades range from painted concrete masonry unit (CMU) blocks to corrugated metal cladding and board-formed concrete, reflecting the pragmatic material culture of postwar industrial construction. The typology sits directly on the street edge in dense urban industrial zones, with raised dock platforms and overhead doors defining the public face. Contemporary adaptations increasingly reinterpret the form with expressive structure — glulam arches, glazed gable ends — while retaining the single-storey large-span interior logic.

source_families.title: Modern Big Box Logistics
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Modern big-box logistics facilities are large-footprint, single- or multi-storey warehouse and distribution buildings optimised for freight throughput, pallet storage, and last-mile or regional supply-chain operations. Their defining architectural features are repetitive dock-door bays along long operational facades, clear-span structural systems allowing column-free interiors, and a compact office or reception pod articulated in glazing at the building corner or entrance. The typology ranges from compact urban infill distribution centres with multi-level truck ramps to sprawling single-storey fulfilment sheds on suburban logistics parks, reflecting the full spectrum of e-commerce and industrial supply-chain demand. Facades are typically tilt-up concrete, insulated metal cladding, or composite panel systems with minimal ornamentation, expressing an honest industrial aesthetic tempered by branding, landscaping, and occasional biophilic gestures on contemporary examples.

source_families.title: Outdoor Sports Stadium
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The outdoor sports stadium typology encompasses large-footprint spectator venues designed around an open playing field, with tiered seating bowls rising from street level to form a continuous or segmented ring. These structures serve as civic landmarks, anchoring neighborhoods with monumental scale and high pedestrian activity on event days. Architecturally, they range from expressive high-tech steel-and-ETFE shells to heritage brick arenas, biophilic mass-timber bowls, and utilitarian exposed-steel grandstands, each reflecting the era and ambition of their commissioning city. The exterior facade wraps the seating bowl and back-of-house concourses, functioning as a billboard-scale urban presence visible from surrounding streets and transit corridors. Program typically includes ticketing gates, concession concourses, press boxes, VIP suites, and at larger scales, integrated retail or hospitality at grade.

source_families.title: Parisian Mid Rise
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Parisian mid-rise is a quintessential European urban building type defined by Haussmann-era proportion, stone facades, and the seamless integration of ground-floor commerce with upper-floor residential or office use. Typically five to seven storeys, these perimeter-block buildings line boulevards with a continuous street wall punctuated by wrought-iron balconies, tall double-hung windows, and a mansard or zinc-clad attic storey. The typology spans from canonical Second Empire limestone blocks to Art Nouveau corner pieces, early-20th-century brick variants, and contemporary hybrid retrofits that graft glass penthouses onto historic stone plinths. Ground floors open generously to the pavement through arched arcade bays, shopfronts with canvas awnings, or glazed retail galleries, animating the street at all hours. The archetype anchors urban grain, enforces boulevard alignment, and projects civic elegance through material richness and tectonic restraint.

source_families.title: Parkitecture
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Parkitecture refers to the rustic architectural style developed by the United States National Park Service in the early twentieth century, blending hand-hewn log construction, rough-cut stone masonry, and heavy timber framing into buildings that feel organically rooted in their natural surroundings. The typology encompasses visitor centers, ranger stations, lodges, and recreational facilities designed to harmonize with wilderness landscapes while providing durable public amenities. Characterized by generous covered porches, massive stone chimneys, steeply pitched shingle or shake roofs, and exposed structural timbers, these structures project an aesthetic of rugged craftsmanship and romantic naturalism. The style spans scales from a single-story frontier cabin to a multi-story lodge complex, unified by the consistent use of unfinished local materials and a warm, earthen palette. Parkitecture remains a beloved and widely reproduced vernacular for recreational facilities, park gatehouses, and nature-adjacent civic buildings.

source_families.title: Postmodern Community Rec Centre
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The postmodern community recreation centre is a civic building typology that prioritises expressive architectural identity over functional anonymity, signalling public ownership through bold form, colour, and material play. Programs typically include gymnasiums, multi-purpose halls, fitness suites, aquatic facilities, and community meeting rooms arranged around a legible public entry sequence. The archetype spans a wide stylistic range — from exuberant primary-colour panelled volumes with porthole windows to contextual brick pavilions with patterned brickwork, to parametric deconstructivist metal-clad forms and sculptural concrete shells with geometric apertures. Common to all variants is a strong street presence, a clearly articulated main entrance, and a civic generosity of scale that distinguishes the building from its residential and commercial neighbours. The typology celebrates architecture as community identity-making, treating the building facade as a communicative surface.

source_families.title: Regional Hospital / Medical Center
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A regional hospital or medical center serving as the primary acute-care facility for a district or catchment area. Programmed with inpatient wards, emergency department, operating theatres, diagnostic imaging, outpatient clinics, and administrative offices. Architectural expression spans heritage pavilion-style pride, utilitarian mid-century district hospitals, contemporary teaching-hospital complexes, and new biophilic wellness-focused facilities — a building type with remarkable stylistic range driven by era, clinical philosophy, and site constraints.

source_families.title: Research Laboratory
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Research laboratories encompass a broad spectrum of building typologies united by the demand for highly serviced, technically complex interiors supporting scientific investigation, experimentation, and discovery. Programs range from wet chemistry and biology labs to physics instrumentation suites, cleanrooms, and computational research facilities, often requiring deep floor plates, generous floor-to-floor heights, and robust mechanical infrastructure. Architecturally the typology ranges from expressive high-tech glass-and-steel structures that celebrate their mechanical systems to neoclassical collegiate institutions, biophilic mass-timber campuses, and utilitarian brutalist containment facilities. The building's character is frequently shaped by the tension between transparency and security, between openness to collaboration and the containment requirements of hazardous research. Across all variants, robust MEP infrastructure — exhaust stacks, fume hoods, chilled-water risers — is a defining architectural signature.

source_families.title: Research Laboratory Innovation Hub
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Research Laboratory Innovation Hub is an institutional building type that combines advanced scientific research facilities with collaborative innovation spaces, typically serving universities, biotech clusters, or public research agencies. These buildings balance highly serviced wet and dry lab floors with open co-working zones, seminar rooms, and maker spaces, promoting cross-disciplinary exchange. Architecturally, they range from stacked contemporary volumes with generous glazing to monolithic brutalist concrete frames with exposed structure, reflecting the intellectual rigor of their programs. The typology often incorporates rooftop greenhouses, solar canopies, or biophilic elements as signals of sustainability-focused research missions. Street-level activation through glazed lobbies and café frontages connects the institution to the urban fabric.

source_families.title: Residential Superblock
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The residential superblock is a large-footprint, mid-rise apartment typology that occupies one or more full city blocks, providing high-density housing within a unified architectural composition. These buildings typically consolidate ground-floor retail or civic uses beneath stacked residential floors, with shared courtyard or roof amenities buffering the interior from the street. The typology spans a wide range of architectural movements — from parametric sculptural forms and Haussmann-era classical blocks to mass-timber biophilic complexes and brutalist megastructures — unified by their monumental urban scale and perimeter block logic. Facades are designed to address the street continuously, maintaining an active edge condition while upper floors step back, cantilever, or articulate to reduce visual bulk. As a cornerstone of urban residential density strategies, the superblock balances neighborhood-scale presence with internal community amenity.

source_families.title: Science Engineering Lab Complex
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A science and engineering laboratory complex is a purpose-built academic research facility designed to house wet and dry labs, collaborative maker spaces, lecture halls, and faculty offices within a single integrated building. These complexes typically prioritize flexible open floor plates, robust MEP infrastructure for fume hoods and specialized equipment, and generous glazing to promote visibility into active research spaces. Architecturally they range from expressive parametric forms signaling institutional ambition to restrained brutalist blocks valued for structural pragmatism, to contemporary mass-timber hybrids reflecting sustainability mandates. The building type occupies a prominent position on university campuses or urban research districts, often serving as a gateway structure that communicates the institution's scientific identity to the public realm.

source_families.title: Second Empire Civic Building
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Second Empire Civic Building is a monumental institutional typology drawn from mid-to-late 19th-century French-influenced American civic architecture, characterized by its signature mansard roof, rusticated stone base, and hierarchical facade composition. These structures served as courthouses, city halls, post offices, fire stations, and municipal offices — embodying civic authority through classical ornamentation, projecting pavilions, and prominent corner or central clock towers. Facades are composed of dressed limestone or granite ashlar, articulated by cornices, pilasters, arched window surrounds, and sculptural relief panels. The mansard roofline — clad in slate or standing-seam metal with dormer windows — provides a distinctive silhouette that signals civic importance on the urban skyline. Buildings of this type anchor civic squares and major street corners, typically set back behind balustrades, grand entry stairs, and street-tree plantings.

source_families.title: Student Residence Tower
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Student residence towers are purpose-built vertical housing typologies serving university and college populations, combining private sleeping units with shared amenity floors, study lounges, dining, and ground-level activation. These buildings typically occupy urban infill or campus-edge sites, rising between 8 and 14 storeys to maximize bed counts on constrained footprints. Architectural expression ranges from biophilic mass-timber and curtain-wall hybrids to raw board-formed concrete brutalist slabs, reflecting differing institutional philosophies around student life and sustainability. Ground floors are consistently activated with transparent glazing revealing common rooms, fitness centres, or retail, reinforcing pedestrian engagement along the street. The typology prioritizes communal identity, durable materiality, and a legible public presence befitting an institutional landmark.

source_families.title: Student Union Campus Centre
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The Student Union Campus Centre serves as the social and civic heart of a university campus, consolidating student services, dining, gathering spaces, clubs, and informal study zones under one roof. These buildings are characterised by generous public interiors, expressive architectural gestures that signal welcome and identity, and a strong relationship to campus pedestrian networks. Programmatically they balance large-span social halls with intimate breakout spaces, often incorporating cafes, event venues, and student government offices. Architecturally they range from expressive mass-timber biophilic complexes to brutalist concrete landmarks, reflecting the era and institutional culture of their campus. Their frontages are typically highly transparent at ground level to draw students in from surrounding quads and streets.

source_families.title: Ttc Streetcar Platform Stop
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The TTC Streetcar Platform Stop is a mid-block transit infrastructure typology representing Toronto's surface rapid transit network, providing sheltered boarding platforms embedded within street rights-of-way. These stops range from enclosed heritage-character shelters to open-air contemporary canopy structures, all designed to serve the Bombardier Flexity low-floor streetcar fleet operating on dedicated or shared track. Architecturally the typology spans over a century of transit design language, from red-brick and patinated-copper heritage pavilions to sleek glass-and-aluminum contemporary enclosures and biophilic green-roof canopies. Each variant prioritizes passenger weather protection, wayfinding signage, tactile platform edges, and clear sightlines to approaching vehicles. The stops function as small-scale civic anchors along commercial corridors, reinforcing the identity of Toronto's mixed-use street fabric.

source_families.title: University Academic Complex
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The University Academic Complex archetype encompasses the full spectrum of higher-education building typologies, from landmark heritage halls to cutting-edge parametric research pavilions. These structures house lecture theatres, seminar rooms, faculty offices, libraries, and interdisciplinary laboratories within massing that ranges from compact urban infill blocks to sprawling classical colonnades. Architecturally the typology is defined by a strong institutional presence on the street, legible entry sequences, and facades that communicate civic purpose — whether through carved limestone ornament, biophilic mass-timber screens, or solar-integrated curtain wall. Sustainability credentials are increasingly embedded in the building fabric itself, with living walls, green roofs, and exposed structural systems becoming markers of progressive academic identity. The four variants represented here span neoclassical Georgian, contemporary high-tech, biophilic mass-timber, and brutalist-industrial research-lab expressions.

source_families.title: University Library
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: The university library is a major civic-institutional anchor on campus, providing collections, collaborative study, digital research, and community gathering under one roof. These buildings are defined by their architectural ambition — each generation of university library reflects the design values of its era, from Brutalist concrete fortresses to biophilic mass-timber pavilions. Facades range from sculptural corten arches and patterned glass curtainwalls to load-bearing stone roundhouses with ceremonial forecourts. Street presence is deliberate and monumental, with generous entrance stairs, transparent ground floors revealing reading rooms within, and carefully landscaped public approaches. The typology balances institutional gravitas with inviting permeability, signaling intellectual openness to the broader campus and city.

source_families.title: Vertical Farm Indoor Agriculture
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Vertical farm indoor agriculture buildings integrate controlled-environment crop production into urban structures, stacking hydroponic or aeroponic growing layers across multiple floors to produce food within or adjacent to city populations. These buildings range from mid-rise glass curtain-wall towers with visible grow-lighting and robotic equipment to low-rise industrial retrofits topped with rooftop glasshouses, each expressing their agricultural program through transparency, grow-light glow, or greenhouse superstructures. Facades often reveal the interior farming operations — lush green plant rows, LED grow-light arrays, and automated racking systems — blurring the boundary between food production and urban spectacle. The typology can take the form of a sleek contemporary tower, a compact opaque controlled-environment block, a mass-timber high-rise, or an adaptive reuse of legacy industrial fabric. As urban food resilience becomes a planning priority, vertical farms are increasingly treated as civic infrastructure with public-facing ground-floor retail and educational programs.

source_families.title: Vertiport Evtol Facility
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A vertiport and eVTOL facility is a next-generation air mobility transit hub designed to receive, charge, and dispatch electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft within or adjacent to the urban fabric. The typology blends terminal building functions — passenger check-in, waiting lounges, and ground-side connectivity — with rooftop or elevated landing pads engineered for rotorcraft clearance and noise attenuation. Architecturally, vertiports range from compact infill termini integrated into existing transit nodes to freestanding contemporary towers with dedicated rooftop flight decks. The building program typically includes ticketing and lounge space, eVTOL charging bays, operations control rooms, and intermodal connections to rail, bus, and ride-share. As a nascent typology, vertiports draw aesthetic cues from aviation, sustainability, and civic infrastructure — presenting a forward-looking image of urban air mobility.

source_families.title: RNDSQR Missing Middle Townhomes
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Contemporary inner-city Calgary infill townhomes in the manner of RNDSQR's 'missing middle' rowhouse work (in the spirit of Killarney 28, Altadore 50, and Peaks + Plains, designed with MODA and Vera Architecture). A row of three-storey ground-oriented homes sensitively inserted into an established single-family street — denser than a duplex, far smaller than a condo tower. The signature look pairs warm cedar and natural wood with charcoal-black metal panel and textural corrugated steel, crisp high-contrast black-and-white trim, matte-black hardware, and large black-framed windows. Massing is broken into distinct articulated bays so the row reads as individual homes rather than one block, frequently with a 'mountain / plains' juxtaposition of peaked and flat roofs, private rooftop patios, and basement secondary suites tucked underneath for affordability. Draws from RNDSQR's vocabulary rather than copying any single project.

source_families.title: RNDSQR Terraced Mixed-Use Mid-Rise
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: A contemporary 'missing middle' mixed-use mid-rise in the manner of RNDSQR's flagship Calgary work (in the spirit of Courtyard 33 in Marda Loop, GROW and Village in Bankview, and the RNDSQR Block in Inglewood, designed with 5468796 Architecture and MODA). Four to six storeys is the norm, stepping down to two or three at the street corner and climbing toward the rear so it reads as several terraced masses rather than one block. A restrained palette of charcoal-black metal panel and corrugated steel is warmed by natural wood and brick; the ground floor is a fully glazed, active retail and restaurant frontage, often opening onto an elevated central courtyard — a 'neighbourhood living room' reached by a wide public stair. Recessed and lightly cantilevered balconies, an articulated almost 'pixelated' roofscape of pitched and flat planes, rooftop terraces and gardens, and local-artist murals complete the language. Resembles RNDSQR's vocabulary rather than copying any single building.

source_families.title: Rural Gas Station

A flat steel fuel canopy on slender columns shelters several pump islands in front of a low convenience-store box with glazed storefront and bright fascia branding. A tall internally-lit price pylon stands at the road, with a paved apron, air/vacuum bay, and propane cage to the side. Set against an open prairie horizon with big sky and a distant grain elevator.

source_families.description: A low-rise commercial strip mall typical of Canadian suburban arterials and prairie highway towns. A long single- or two-storey retail bar with a continuous covered sidewalk fronts a large parking apron, divided into a row of tenant bays — a grocery or pharmacy anchor at one end and smaller units (restaurant, salon, dollar store, clinic) along the run. A flat roof hides behind a signage parapet, with backlit tenant signs and a shared pylon at the road.

Guest-room wings (one to four storeys) wrap a parking lot, with exterior or interior corridors, a small office/lobby and breakfast room, a porte-cochère at the larger formats, and a tall illuminated roadside sign. Practical, durable construction set against an open prairie horizon.

source_families.title: Road Diet Complete Street

source_families.title: Two-Stage Crossing Median (Pedestrian Refuge)

On this 16 m collector exemplar, every crosswalk is RAISED — a flat-topped plateau 75–90 mm above the roadway in NACTO's speed-table geometry (6.7 m long with ramped approaches), surfaced in contrasting unit pavers. Pedestrians cross at sidewalk level; vehicles yield by geometry, crossing at 25–30 km/h. Operating speed follows table spacing — the design lever for a 30 km/h school-area collector.

Priority is encoded physically rather than with signs; this is default design in the Netherlands. Paired with warm brick sidewalk surfacing, tight 3 m corner radii and boulevard planting.

The treatment for downtown junctions where pedestrian volumes rival or exceed vehicle volumes; corner curb extensions provide the queuing space the all-walk surge needs.

One of the cheapest sightline treatments in the toolkit — Hoboken NJ paired citywide daylighting with years of zero traffic deaths.

source_families.title: Left Turn Calming Intersection
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: NYC Vision Zero signature treatment: HARDENED CENTRELINES — low rubber curbing with flexible posts along the centreline through the junction box — plus slow-turn wedges force left-turning drivers into a square, slow turn instead of cutting the corner at speed across the crosswalk. Left turns are among the most dangerous pedestrian conflicts at signalized intersections; this geometry takes the fast diagonal path away.

source_families.title: Neighborhood Gateway
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Gateway treatment for a local street mouth (NACTO neckdown geometry): paired planted curb extensions pinch the entry to a single comfortable car width, a raised paver entry table lifts the crossing to sidewalk level, and gateway planting announces the 30 km/h neighbourhood beyond. Deployed at every local mouth off a collector, it tells drivers the rules changed at the property line — before the first house, not after.

source_families.title: Neighborhood Greenway
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Bicycle boulevard / neighbourhood greenway (NACTO Urban Bikeway Design Guide): an ordinary low-volume residential street turned into a low-stress bike and walking spine without separated lanes — large sharrow + green bicycle stencils claim the centre of each lane, speed humps and a planted mini circle keep cars under 30 km/h, and where the greenway meets a busy street it gets a protected median crossing. Best where motor volumes are already low (under ~1,500 vehicles/day); the calm comes from removing through-traffic, not from a curb.

source_families.title: Diverter (Modal Filter)
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Low-Traffic-Neighbourhood modal filter (NACTO diverters; Dutch 'knip'): a point treatment on a residential street that blocks through MOTOR traffic while leaving a clear gap for people walking and cycling. It removes rat-running without removing access — drivers can still reach every address, just not cut through. Three forms as variants: a diagonal diverter that forces all cars to turn at a four-way, a partial (half) closure that blocks one direction of entry, and a median filter that lets a side street cross or turn but not pass straight through an arterial.

source_families.title: Neighborhood Traffic Circle
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Neighbourhood traffic circle (NACTO; TAC Canadian Guide to Traffic Calming): a small planted island dropped into the middle of a residential four-way intersection, replacing stop signs with a slow yield-around movement. Drivers must steer around it, which cuts entry speeds and the right-angle and left-turn crashes that plague uncontrolled local intersections — Seattle's thousand-plus circles are the classic precedent. Smaller and simpler than a roundabout: no splitter islands, often a mountable apron, and a garden at its heart. Per Calgary Street Manual sec. 10.4.4.4, neighbourhood traffic circles are used only at Local-street intersections and typically fit within the existing intersection footprint without moving the curb lines.

source_families.title: Raised Intersection
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Raised intersection (NACTO Urban Street Design Guide): the entire junction is lifted to sidewalk level on a single flat-topped plateau, with ramps on every approach, so pedestrians cross level in all directions and vehicles slow to climb and traverse the whole crossing. Surfaced in contrasting unit pavers, it reads as a continuous pedestrian zone the cars are guests on — ideal for neighbourhood-commercial corners and residential collectors with heavy walking.

source_families.title: Advisory Bike Lane Street
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Advisory bike lane / edge lane road (TAC; FHWA advisory shoulders): a residential street too narrow for full bike lanes plus two travel lanes is striped with DASHED bike lanes on both edges and a single central two-way motor lane. Cars drive in the centre and, when meeting oncoming traffic, briefly merge into the dashed bike lane after yielding to any cyclist. Gives people on bikes a marked place on streets that otherwise could not fit them, at low cost — common in the Netherlands and growing in Canadian cities.

source_families.title: Speed Cushion Street
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Speed cushion street (NACTO; TAC Canadian Guide to Traffic Calming): vertical speed control sized for streets that fire trucks and buses use. Each cushion is a raised pad that fills only the middle of a travel lane, with wheel gaps at the centreline and curb — narrow-track cars must slow to ride over it, but wide-axle fire apparatus and buses straddle the gaps and pass unimpeded. The way to calm a residential emergency-response or transit route without delaying the responders.

source_families.title: Speed Hump (Local Street)
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Speed hump local street (Calgary Street Manual sec. 10.4.3.2; TAC Canadian Guide to Traffic Calming): the City's standard vertical calming device for residential Local streets. A rounded asphalt hump 75–90 mm high and 4.0 m long spans the full travel lane with no wheel gaps, so every car must ease over it. Calgary uses the 4.0 m hump rather than a speed table in 30 km/h zones (vehicles cross tables too fast), and unlike a speed cushion it has no cut-outs — so it is for Local streets without bus or primary fire-response routes. Humps sit at least 10 m clear of crossings and intersections, 75 m from signals, and are spaced 100 m apart so operating speed settles around 30 km/h.

source_families.title: High-Entry-Angle Right Turn
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: High-entry-angle right turn (Calgary Street Manual sec. 10.4.4.5 / 9.7.3.1): a channelized right-turn geometry used on Arterial and Collector-Industrial intersection approaches where a free-flowing slip lane would carry drivers around the corner too fast. A raised triangular channelizing island steers the right-turning driver to meet the cross street at a high, near-perpendicular angle, so they slow to a yield condition and turn their head to see people walking and wheeling crossing the short island leg. It replaces the wide, fast, sweeping slip lane with a tight, deliberate, low-speed right turn.

source_families.title: Right-In Right-Out Median
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Right-in/right-out access control median (Calgary Street Manual sec. 10.4.5.1): a continuous raised median along a Collector or Arterial street that physically prevents left turns and straight-across movements to and from minor approaches and commercial driveways. Drivers entering or leaving an access can only turn right; left turns are consolidated at controlled intersections or dedicated median openings with turn bays. By removing the most conflict-prone movements, it cuts angle and turning crashes along busy commercial frontages while keeping traffic flowing.

source_families.title: Directional / Full Closure
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Directional and full closures (Calgary Street Manual sec. 10.4.5.3): volume-management closures used on Local streets to cut short-cutting traffic, usually as part of a neighbourhood or corridor traffic-calming project. A directional closure uses a raised island or curb to block selected movements (e.g. no through, or no left) at an intersection while keeping others open; a full closure caps a street leg entirely with a landscaped barrier and turnaround. Both keep a clear bollarded gap for people walking and wheeling and a mountable or removable section for emergency access, so motor volumes drop while the active-transportation and emergency network stays whole.

source_families.title: Protected Bike Lane (Bi-Directional)
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: Bi-directional protected bicycle lane (Alberta Bicycle Facilities Design Guide; Calgary Street Manual sec. 5.2.1.2 two-way cycle track): a two-way cycle track carried on ONE side of the street, physically separated from motor traffic by a raised curb, planted buffer or parking lane, with people cycling in BOTH directions side by side across a painted centre line. Concentrating the facility on one side is efficient where destinations, a river pathway, or intersection geometry favour that side, and it is delineated from the sidewalk so people walking and wheeling stay separate. Target running width about 3.6 m (3.0 m minimum when constrained) plus a buffer to the travel lane; used on Collectors and Arterials as part of the primary cycling network.

source_families.title: Bicycle Shared Space
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Bicycle shared space (Alberta Bicycle Facilities Design Guide; Calgary Street Manual sec. 5.2.3 local street bikeway): the lowest-separation on-street bikeway, where people cycling share the travel lane with motor traffic on a low-volume, low-speed Local street. There is no dedicated bike lane; instead shared-lane markings (sharrows) and wayfinding signs position riders and signal drivers to expect bikes. Used only where motor volumes and speeds are low enough (about 30 km/h) that mixing is comfortable for all ages.

source_families.title: Bicycle Lane (Painted)
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Painted bicycle lane (Alberta Bicycle Facilities Design Guide; Calgary Street Manual sec. 5.2.4): an on-street bike lane delineated from the travel lane by paint only — a solid white line, bike symbols and (where space allows) a striped buffer — with no physical separation. One lane runs each way beside the travel lanes. The unbuffered lane is the minimum treatment (~1.5–1.8 m); the buffered lane adds a painted buffer (~0.6 m) for extra comfort beside faster or busier traffic. Suited to Collectors and lower-speed Arterials where a protected lane is not yet feasible.

source_families.title: Bicycle Accessible Shoulder
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Bicycle accessible shoulder (Alberta Bicycle Facilities Design Guide): a paved shoulder on a rural or semi-rural road wide enough to be ridden comfortably, the standard cycling provision outside curbed urban areas. There is no curb or sidewalk; a sealed paved shoulder (about 1.5 m, wider on higher-speed roads) runs each side between the travel lane edge line and the gravel verge / drainage ditch, giving people cycling a usable surface separated from traffic by an edge line and rumble strip rather than a barrier.

source_families.title: Bicycle Pathway
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Bicycle pathway (Alberta Bicycle Facilities Design Guide; Calgary Street Manual sec. 5.2.2): a paved off-street path reserved for cycling, away from motor traffic, typically through a park, utility corridor or along a greenway. Unlike a multi-use pathway it is bike-priority — about 3.0–4.0 m wide with a painted centre line for two-way riding and (where pedestrian volumes warrant) a separate adjacent walking path. Grass or naturalized verges run each side. It forms the comfortable, uninterrupted spine of the cycling network between on-street connections.

source_families.title: Protected Intersection (Diagram)
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: Protected intersection authored from the engineered PLAN DIAGRAM (Calgary Street Manual Fig 9.14; derived from the City of Ottawa Protected Intersection Design Guide) rather than a photo. Corner refuge islands set the bike and pedestrian crossings back from the corner, one-way protected bike tracks wrap each corner behind the islands, and the set-back crossings give drivers a near-square, slow turn with clear sightlines to people walking and wheeling. Its reference image is a buildings-free technical diagram, so the render reproduces only the junction geometry — no invented streetwall or phantom buildings.

source_families.description: Compact single-lane roundabout authored from a clean engineered PLAN diagram rather than a photo: a planted central island and tight circulating roadway slow every movement to a low speed, raised splitter islands on each approach deflect entry and double as pedestrian refuges, and set-back zebra crossings span each leg. Its reference image is a buildings-free technical diagram, so the render reproduces only the junction geometry — no invented streetwall or phantom buildings.

source_families.title: Curb Extension Crossing (Diagram)

source_families.description: Mid-block pedestrian crossing with curb extensions (bulb-outs) authored from a clean engineered PLAN diagram: the sidewalk is extended into the parking lane on both sides to shorten the crossing distance, tighten the effective roadway and improve sightlines between people walking and drivers, with a continental (ladder) crosswalk between the bulb-outs. Its reference image is a buildings-free technical diagram, so the render reproduces only the street and crossing geometry — no invented streetwall or phantom buildings.

source_families.title: Lake Edge Plaza

source_families.description: A hard-paved urban plaza meeting a flat lake edge — formal stone esplanade or terrace with a continuous lake-side parapet, lining the urban edge of a major lake or large reservoir

source_families.title: Academic Courtyard
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A small enclosed courtyard nestled between academic buildings, offering a quiet outdoor room for study and gathering. Paved seating areas, raised planters of ornamental grasses and small trees, and a sculptural feature or canopy fill a compact rectangle framed on most sides by building walls, threaded by short paths between entrances.

source_families.title: Airport Airfield
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: An airport or airfield: long paved runways and taxiways serving aircraft parked on concrete aprons beside terminal buildings and hangars. Marked runway thresholds and centrelines, taxiway networks, fuel and service areas, and landside roads and car parks complete the complex. Scale ranges from a small general-aviation field with a single short strip to a major multi-runway commercial hub.

source_families.title: Athletics Precinct Sports Fields
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: An outdoor athletics and playing-field precinct: a cluster of full-size rectangular sports pitches and oval fields served by a clubhouse or grandstand, floodlight masts, and paved entry plazas. Mown turf fields with crisp white markings dominate, edged by spectator seating, warm-up areas, and perimeter trees, with a brick or modern fieldhouse anchoring one end.

source_families.title: Campus Central Quad
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: The central open quadrangle of a university or institutional campus, framed by academic buildings and serving as its social heart. A generous lawn or planted ground plane is crossed by gathering paths, shaded by trees, and dotted with seating, with a focal lawn, fountain, or garden at the centre. Character ranges from naturalized meadow to formal collegiate green to modern hardscape plaza.

source_families.title: Campus Pedestrian Spine
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A long linear pedestrian promenade forming the main movement corridor of a campus or district, running between flanking buildings. A broad central walkway is lined with street trees, planting strips, benches, and lighting, occasionally widening into small plazas or punctuated by a pavilion or pergola. Character ranges from a green planted spine to an urban paved street to a garden walk.

source_families.title: Constructed Wetland Eco Park
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A constructed wetland park that treats and slows water while creating habitat and public space. Shallow planted cells of reeds and sedges, open ponds, and meandering channels are linked by boardwalks and viewing decks, framed by meadow banks and a nature pavilion. From above it reads as a mosaic of water, reed bed, and path winding between built edges.

source_families.title: Equestrian Center
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A working equestrian centre organised around riding arenas, stable barns, and fenced turnout paddocks. Sand-surfaced dressage and jumping arenas sit beside gable-roofed stable blocks, circular round pens, horse-trailer parking, and hay and manure stores, the whole site stitched together by service lanes and white post-and-rail fencing.

source_families.title: Golf Course 18 Hole
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A full 18-hole golf course sprawling across roughly fifty to seventy-five hectares of manicured turf. Winding green fairways and circular putting greens are punctuated by pale sand bunkers, ponds and water hazards, and stands of mature trees, threaded by looping cart paths and anchored by a clubhouse with its practice putting green and parking. Character ranges from seaside links to parkland, desert, and modern championship layouts.

source_families.title: Golf Driving Range
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A golf driving range built around a long open grass landing field fronted by a row of hitting bays. Golfers tee off from a covered or two-tier bay structure toward distance markers and target greens spread down a deep mown corridor netted along its sides, with a small pro shop, putting green, and parking at the front. Forms range from a simple covered range to a multi-level entertainment venue.

source_families.title: Mountain Bike Park
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A mountain-bike facility built from sculpted earth: pump tracks, dirt-jump lines, bermed flow trails, and skills features shaped into the ground. Looping ribbons of asphalt or hard-packed dirt wind between mounds, rollers, and tabletops, with a small lodge or shelter, bike racks, and seating at the entry. Forms range from a compact urban pump track to a hillside bike park laced with trails.

source_families.title: Multi Sport Complex
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A clustered multi-sport recreation complex combining indoor sports buildings with outdoor fields and courts. A large fieldhouse, stadium grandstand, or fabric-domed arena anchors the site beside full-size playing pitches, hardcourt batteries, a running track, paved entry plazas, and deep parking aprons, the whole campus linked by walkways and dotted with floodlight masts.

source_families.title: Research Garden Teaching Arboretum
source_families.scope: Exact current variants mapped above; other variants unreviewed
source_families.description: A botanical research garden and teaching arboretum where labelled plant collections double as living laboratory and public landscape. Curated tree groves, themed planting beds, glasshouses, and demonstration plots are organised along interpretive paths with signage and seating, anchored by a research pavilion or conservatory. Forms range from a sprawling tree-collection arboretum to a compact greenhouse research garden.

source_families.title: Rewilding Ecological Restoration Zone
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A landscape-scale zone given over to ecological recovery, where degraded or vacant land is restored to native habitat. Tall grass prairie, regenerating woodland, wetland, and riparian edges establish over time, with minimal infrastructure — a few boardwalks, overlooks, and interpretive nodes — and sometimes conservation grazing animals. From above it reads as wide, textured, low-intervention nature rather than designed parkland.

source_families.title: Stormwater Naturalized Drainage Corridor
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A linear naturalized drainage corridor that carries and cleans stormwater along a green ribbon through the urban fabric. A meandering channel or daylit stream runs the length, flanked by sloped meadow and shrub banks, bioswales, and a walking path with footbridges. Forms range from a soft naturalized creek to a stepped urban daylit channel.

source_families.title: Stormwater Resilience Park
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A multifunctional park engineered to capture, store, and slow stormwater while serving as everyday public space. Terraced detention basins, bioswales, and rain gardens hold water after storms and become planted lawns and meadows when dry, threaded by boardwalks and paths. Forms range from urban bioswale parks to naturalistic detention basins to engineered terraced water plazas.

source_families.title: Velodrome Cycling Track
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A velodrome built around a steeply banked oval cycling track enclosing a flat infield. The elongated track reads from above as a rounded-rectangle ring, wrapped by tiered spectator seating or a sweeping arena roof, with a timing tower, warm-up apron, and entry plaza alongside. Forms range from open-air concrete tracks to iconic timber-roofed indoor arenas.

source_families.title: Suburban Retail Parking Lot
source_families.scope: Inventoried only; not individually classified or asserted available
source_families.description: A large suburban retail parking lot serving a strip mall, big-box store, gas station, or roadside hotel. A broad asphalt field of painted stalls and wide drive aisles fronts the storefronts, with cart corrals, accessible stalls near the entrance, pole-mounted area lighting, scattered landscaped islands, and a tall pylon sign at the highway edge. Typical of Canadian prairie-town commercial strips and highway service nodes.
